entries.title: John
entries.content:
In the beginning: Using the same phrase as the beginning of the Old Testament (Genesis 1:1), the Gospel of John introduces Jesus Christ as the one through whom God created everything (John 1:3). Through Jesus, God also creates new life in those who believe (John 1:12–13). 

The Gospel of John begins with its central claim: Jesus Christ, the Word (logos), not only revealed God but was God. The Greek word logos means “word” or “message.” The logos is the Word of God, through whom God created everything, made himself known, and became human as Jesus Christ. Later Christian teaching describes the Word as the second person of the Trinity (the one who shares fully in God’s nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit).

In Greek thought, the logos was the rational principle that ordered the universe and made life understandable. It explained why the world had meaning and structure.

For Jewish people, the logos was the word of the Lord. It expressed God’s wisdom and God’s creative power. God spoke, and things came into being.

By the time of Jesus, people understood the logos as coming from God and sharing God’s character and authority (see Psalm 33:6, Psalms 33:9; Proverbs 8:22–31). John affirmed this understanding by declaring that "the Word [logos] became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The start of this introduction might be a poem or hymn sung by early Christians (John 1:1–5). 

The themes of this introduction of the Gospel of John prepare readers for the story that follows:

• The arrival of the light in the world.

• The rejection of the light.

• The gift of new life given by the light to those who believed in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Word (logos) is God (John 1:1–2). Everything God does, the Word also does. Throughout his Gospel, John presents the actions of Jesus as the actions of God himself.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In Him was life: Life was God’s original gift to his creatures at creation (Genesis 1:20–28; Genesis 2:7). Now the logos gives people the possibility of new life, which comes through rebirth from God (John 1:13). This means receiving new life from God, not a second physical birth. It describes a spiritual beginning in which God gives people new life through faith, making them his children

• As one of his first creative acts, God brought light into the world (Genesis 1:3). In the re-creation of humankind through Jesus Christ, God offered light and life again. Light is a key theme throughout the Gospel of John.

entries.title: John
entries.content: God created light and removed the darkness (Genesis 1:2–5). The darkness resists God (John 3:19–21; John 12:35; Matthew 6:23; Acts 26:17–18; Ephesians 4:17–19; Ephesians 5:7–14; 2 Peter 1:19; 1 John 1:5–7; 1 John 2:9–11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: the darkness has not overcome it: Or the darkness has not understood it; literally, the darkness cannot grasp it. The Greek word katalambanō (“grasp”) can mean either “understand” or “be hostile.” In John’s Gospel, it means "hostility." The darkness would try to destroy Jesus (the Light), but it would fail. The Light would successfully bring salvation to the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: God sent a man named John the Baptist to announce the arrival of Jesus. He prepared people to accept Jesus as God's Son and Messiah (see John 1:19–37; Luke 1:5–25, Luke 1:57–80; Luke 3:1–22). His work fulfilled what God had promised through the prophets (see Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 4:5–6).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Some Jews thought John the Baptist might be the Messiah (God's chosen one). Some of his followers hesitated to follow Jesus (John 3:22–30). However, John the Baptist was not the Light. His role was to announce Jesus (John 1:19–34).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The world does not recognize the true light, even when meeting its Creator. The world lives in rebellion, loving darkness more than light (John 3:19).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• People can follow the light and join God's family only when God spiritually renews them (John 3:1–17). 

• People must believe in Christ to become children of God (John 12:35–36).

entries.title: John
entries.content: born of God: People can escape the darkness only by God’s grace (see John 8:12; John 12:35–36, John 12:44–46).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The Word became flesh: This means the Word became truly human. The idea that the Word became human was shocking to both Greeks and Jews. 

Many Greeks believed that God was completely separate from the ordinary human world. They used the word sarx (Greek for “flesh”) to describe human life as weak or earthly. John taught something very different. He said that God himself became human in Jesus Christ (compare John 1:1). 

Jesus was fully human and fully divine. He was not partly God and partly human. These two truths together form the foundation of Christian teaching about Christ.

• the Word … made His dwelling among us (Greek skēnoō, “pitched a tent”): The Greek verb skēnoō means “to pitch a tent” or “to live in a tent.” This word is related to skēnē, the Greek word for the tabernacle. The tabernacle was the tent where the Lord’s glory lived among Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 25:8–9). In Jesus, God’s glory now lived among his people in a new way (Exodus 40:34–38; John 2:11; John 12:23–28, John 12:41; John 17:1–5). 

• Even though the world was dark and hostile, Jesus came to save it. He offered God’s love and faithfulness to the world (John 3:15–17).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
He was before me: In John the Baptist’s culture, older age was respected and honored (Leviticus 19:32). Younger people were expected to honor those who were older, not replace them (contrast Isaiah 3:5). 

By saying that Jesus existed before him, John the Baptist pointed to the greater honor of Jesus. He explained that Jesus existed before creation itself, not just before the birth of John (John 1:1–3).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• the law: This refers to the Torah, the body of instruction given to Moses at Mount Sinai. The Torah taught Israel how to live in faithful relationship with God and with one another.

• God's grace and truth are present in the Torah, but Jesus fully reveals these qualities in his person and power (John 3:16; John 13:1).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• God would not allow Moses to see him directly (Exodus 33:18–20). Only Jesus has seen the Father, so he alone completely knows him and can tell us about him (John 3:32–35; John 14:9–10). 

• but the one and only Son: The Son, who sees the Father, is himself God. The Son is not simply a messenger who knows something about God. John explicitly affirms Christ’s deity. Jesus shares the substance of God’s being.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
John’s Gospel focuses less on John the Baptist compared to the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew 3:1–6; Mark 1:2–6; Luke 1:1–24, Luke 1:57–80; Luke 3:1–13). However, the apostle John wants us to understand that John the Baptist correctly identified and honored Jesus. 

John the Baptist’s disciples leave him to follow Jesus. Jesus continued the work that John had begun. As the ministry of Jesus grew, John’s ministry became smaller, just as John had said (John 3:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus reveals himself to the world through his miracles and teachings. People reacted differently:

• Some wanted to believe in him.

• Others opposed him. 

This division becomes more obvious as the book continues. Jesus ended his public ministry with a final call for people to believe in him (John 12:44–50).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Jews expected the Christ (the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah) to bring spiritual leadership and political redemption to Israel. Both words mean “Anointed One” (a king chosen and set apart by God). They believed this promised leader would guide them back to faithful worship and free them from foreign rule (see Deuteronomy 18:15; see also the Jewish book Psalms of Solomon from the period between the Old and New Testaments).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The people expected Elijah to come before the Messiah (Malachi 4:5). John the Baptist fulfilled this role as the forerunner (the one who prepares the way). However, John said that he was not Elijah himself (see Matthew 11:14; Luke 1:17). 

• Are you the Prophet?: Compare John 6:14; John 7:40–41.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Who are you?: John the Baptist wanted others to know him as a voice of one calling in the wilderness (see Isaiah 40:3).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Pharisees were deeply devoted to the Scriptures and earnestly desired a righteous life. They also believed in the coming Messiah, which explains their questions here. 

Some Pharisees became followers of Jesus, including the apostle Paul (Acts 15:5; Acts 26:5; Philippians 3:5).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jewish baptisms were ritual washings for becoming ceremonially pure following contact with impurity (Leviticus 8:6; Numbers 19:7). 

• John announced the Christ's arrival and required participants to confess their sins and be baptized (Matthew 3:6). Baptism later became the symbol of membership in the kingdom of God (Acts 2:38; see also John 4:1–2).

entries.title: John
entries.content: A slave usually did simple tasks like removing a sandal. A disciple never did these tasks.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The phrase the Lamb of God may refer to the Passover sacrifice of a lamb or to the daily sacrifice in the temple (Exodus 29:38–46; Hebrews 10). See also Revelation 5.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• John the Baptist's second testimony (see John 1:19–23) describes what happened when he baptized Jesus . 

• In the Old Testament, kings and prophets were anointed with the Holy Spirit. These anointings were temporary. They were given for a specific task or time.

By contrast, the Spirit remained on Jesus. His anointing was not temporary. It was permanent (see John 3:34).

entries.title: John
entries.content: the Son of God: Some ancient manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God,” which echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his chosen servant.

entries.title: John
entries.content: This section introduces the model for discipleship in John’s Gospel. Disciples wanted to come and see Jesus, and when they met him, they stayed with him (John 1:39).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Simon is well known in the Gospels, not for his courage and faith, but for his failings (see John 18:15–18, John 18:25–27). Jesus gave him the name Cephas, an Aramaic word that means “rock.” In Greek, this name is Petros. In English, we say Peter. This name pointed to the strong church leader Simon would later become (see Acts 1:1–5:42; Acts 8:1–12:25; Acts 15:1–41).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Galilee was the region of northern Israel around the Sea of Galilee.

• Bethsaida was a village on Galilee's north shore. The name Bethsaida means "house of fishing." It was the home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip. Later, Andrew and Peter moved to Capernaum, a village west of Bethsaida (Mark 1:21, Mark 1:29).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Philip, a Greek name, and Nathanael, a Hebrew name, represent the mix of cultures in Galilee. The message of Jesus reached both groups in Galilee. When Greeks wanted to see Jesus in Jerusalem, they asked Philip (John 12:20–22). 

• Jesus grew up in Nazareth, a mountain village southwest of the Sea of Galilee.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Can anything good come from Nazareth?: People did not think this village was important enough to be the hometown of a great leader (see Matthew 13:53–58).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus described Nathanael as a true Israelite. He said there was no deceit (no dishonesty or trickery) in him.

This may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, whose early life was marked by deceit. Jacob later received the name Israel (see Genesis 25:27–34; Genesis 27:1–36; Genesis 32:22–32). In this way, Nathanael shows what God desires Israel to be. God wants his people to be an honest and faithful people.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus gained Nathanael’s attention by showing that he knew his character (John 1:47). Then Jesus showed that he knew Nathanael’s earlier actions, even though they had not met before.

This supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability) amazed Nathanael. He saw this as a sign from God and responded with faith.

Nathanael had witnessed a miracle. As a result, he made a strong confession about who Jesus is.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Truly, truly (Greek amēn amēn): Jesus often used this phrase to emphasize important points. In John’s Gospel, the Greek word amēn is always doubled. 

• you will all see heaven open: Jesus made the comparison with Jacob clear (see study note on 1:47; see Genesis 28:10–22). Like Jacob, Nathanael would see God at work. Jacob saw a vision at Bethel, where God revealed himself (Genesis 28:19). 

Jesus himself is the new Bethel. The name Bethel means “house of God.” In other words, Jesus is the place where God now lives among his people.

• Son of Man: See study note on John 9:35; see also Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 8:31. 

• John the apostle used several names for Jesus (Son of God, Son of Man, Christ). Knowing the true identity of Jesus is necessary to fully understanding and following him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Wedding ceremonies could last up to a week. They often included dramatic parades where the husband brought the bride to his home for the celebrations (Matthew 25:1–13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: In this section, Jesus appeared at two symbolic Jewish ceremonies. At a wedding in Cana (John 2:1–12), he replaced the ritual cleansing water with his own superior wine. Later, around Passover, he cleansed the temple (John 2:13–25).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus showed who he is and what he came to do through the religious practices and festivals of the Jewish people (see John 2:1; John 5:1). He used these familiar events to reveal his identity and his mission.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• When the wine supply ran out, the host’s family would face embarrassment for failure to plan properly. Perhaps Jesus arrived unexpectedly with his disciples (see Matthew 25:1–13). This might explain why his mother told him about the problem. 

• A wedding feast was a major celebration in Jewish village life. This particular event also symbolized the joy of the Messiah's arrival.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• At first, Jesus did not step in to solve the problem. His mission and its timing were not controlled by human plans.

• My hour has not yet come: This refers to the time when Jesus would be glorified. In the Gospel of John, this happened when he was lifted up on the cross (John 12:23; John 17:1).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The stone water jars were cut from solid rock. They were used for Jewish purification ceremonies (religious washing rituals; see Mark 7:1–4).

Jesus was about to give new meaning to these ceremonies. He would show that something greater than ritual washing was now present.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The master of the banquet repeated a common saying. Normally, the best wine was served first, when people could taste it most clearly. Later, wine of lower quality was served.

But this time it was different. The wine Jesus made, served last, was the best of all.

In the Old Testament, good wine was a sign of God’s blessing(Amos 9:13–14). This miracle showed that the Messiah, God’s greatest blessing, had now come.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus performed this, the first of His signs: In it, he revealed the glory of God (see also John 1:14; John 11:4, John 11:40).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Jewish Passover was an annual spring feast remembering Israel’s rescue from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 12). Jews traveled to Jerusalem to join the feast (Deuteronomy 16:1–16). Because John refers to three Passover feasts (John 2:13; John 6:4; John 11:55), many scholars think Jesus must have had a three-year public ministry.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Many people came to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. They needed animals that met the requirements for sacrifice. The animals had to be approved for worship.

Because of this need, a large business developed. People sold animals and exchanged money for the right kind of coins. However, this buying and selling was taking place in the temple itself.

Jesus acted like a prophet. He demanded that God’s house return to its true purpose. The temple was meant for worship, prayer, teaching, and sacrifice. It was not meant to be a marketplace. This action brought Jesus into conflict with the temple leaders.

• The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) place the clearing out of the temple near the end of the ministry of Jesus (Matthew 21:12–13; Mark 11:15–17; Luke 19:45–46). John might have included this event earlier to emphasize its connection to the miracle where Jesus turned water into wine (John 2:1–11). Both the temple and the stone jars of water were instruments for spiritual purity in Judaism. The jars, once filled with water for ceremonial washing, now held the wine Jesus changed by a miracle. 

In a similar way, the stone temple, which was linked to sacrifice and purification, would no longer be central. Jesus himself would take its place (John 2:19–21). 

Some scholars believe that Jesus cleansed the temple twice. They think he did this once at the beginning of his ministry and again at the end.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Destroy this temple: Herod the Great started rebuilding the temple's grand structure in 20 BC. The work continued until AD 64. This is why Jesus amazed his audience when he claimed he could destroy and rebuild it in a few days. 

However, Jesus was speaking figuratively (using a word picture) about his own body. He described his body as the true temple, the place where God was present (see John 1:14, John 1:51). 

His body would be destroyed. Three days later, God would raise him from the dead. Through his resurrection, Jesus showed that he himself was now the true place where people meet God. Because of this, the Jerusalem Temple and its sacrifices were no longer necessary.

Later, during the trial of Jesus, some people misunderstood his words. They used his statement about destroying the temple as evidence against him. They accused him of blasphemy (Mark 14:58).

entries.title: John
entries.content: they believed: Seeing a miracle from God can lead people to believe. However, this kind of belief is not the deepest faith. The deepest faith trusts Jesus even without seeing miracles (John 20:29).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
John uses a play on words here. Because of Jesus’s signs (miracles that show who he is), many people trusted in him (John 2:23). But Jesus did not trust them in the same way.

This statement does not refer only to certain people in Jerusalem. It shows that Jesus knows what is inside every person. He understands people’s thoughts, motives (reasons for acting), and desires.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• John connects John 2:25 and John 3:1 by using the same Greek word (anthrōpos) to refer to all of humanity and then to a specific man (Nicodemus). 

• Nicodemus had deep religious knowledge. He had also seen what Jesus was doing in Jerusalem (John 2:13–24). But he had not yet experienced spiritual rebirth (a new life that comes from God).

• A Pharisee: See study note on 1:24. The Pharisees were a Jewish group who were careful to obey the law of Moses and their religious traditions.

Nicodemus belonged to this group. He was part of the religious leaders. He was respected for his knowledge of the Jewish law. He likely took pride in his careful obedience and moral purity.

entries.title: John
entries.content: at night: Nicodemus might have been afraid for others to see him with Jesus. In the Gospel of John, night often has a deeper meaning. It can represent evil, error (wrong belief), and unbelief (lack of trust in God; see John 9:4; John 11:10; John 13:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Born again: To experience spiritual birth, God's power must completely renew a person. 

• Nicodemus thought Jesus was speaking about physical birth. He demonstrated that those in darkness, who do not have spiritual rebirth, cannot understand Jesus or other “heavenly things” (John 3:12). 

Jesus sometimes used ironic misunderstanding as a way to teach. He would say something with a deeper spiritual meaning. The listener would misunderstand his words in a simple or physical way. Then Jesus would explain the deeper meaning.

This method helped people see the difference between earthly thinking and spiritual truth.

entries.title: John
entries.content: John the Baptist baptized with water. Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit (John 1:33).

entries.title: John
entries.content: In Greek, the word for wind is the same as for spirit (Greek pneuma). The wind is an appropriate image for the Spirit, who is sent from heaven and cannot be contained or controlled.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
There is a great distance between this world and heaven (see John 1:51; John 3:31; John 6:38, John 6:42). Heaven represents God’s dwelling place. This world represents human life under sin and weakness.

Jesus came down from heaven to this world. He made a way for people to know God. He proved that he came from God when he defeated death. After rising from the dead, he returned to the Father in heaven (John 16:5–11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus was lifted up on the cross so that all people could understand the way of salvation, look to him in faith, and have eternal life.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The truth that God loved the world is basic to Christian understanding (1 John 4:9–10). God's love extends beyond the limits of race and nation, even to those who oppose him (see “The World” Theme Note). 

• The Son came to save, not to condemn, people who often choose spiritual darkness (John 3:17, 19–21).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The original Greek text does not include quotation marks. Because of this, translators must decide where the words of Jesus end and where John's explanation begins. John 3:16–21 might be John’s explanation of what Jesus said.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
As light shines into a dark place, it reveals what was hidden. In the same way, when Jesus came into the world, he exposed its sin and unbelief. Because of this, God’s judgment has already begun.

People who see this light and understand their true condition must respond. They are responsible to believe in God’s Son (John 3:16–17).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
When people live in spiritual darkness (a life separated from God), they do not want the light that Jesus brings. Jesus called himself "the light of the world" (John 8:12; John 9:5). His light shows truth and exposes sin.

Darkness does not simply ignore the light. It resists it and tries to overcome it. But the darkness cannot defeat the light (John 1:5). 

Those who refuse to believe continue to live in darkness (John 13:30). They stumble because they cannot see clearly (John 11:10). In the end, their sins will be revealed. God will judge all people (John 5:28–30; Revelation 20:11–15).

entries.title: John
entries.content: He spent some time with them and baptized: See John 4:2, which explains that the disciples of Jesus were the ones who baptized people.

entries.title: John
entries.content: John the Baptist says Jesus is truly "from above" (John 3:31). So, the followers of John need to start following Jesus instead.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Before King Herod imprisoned John (see Matthew 14:1–12; Mark 1:14; Mark 6:14–29; Luke 3:19–20), he and Jesus were both ministering near the Jordan River. They were working in the same general area.

After John was arrested, Jesus left that region. He traveled north to Galilee and began his ministry there (Mark 1:14).

entries.title: John
entries.content: everyone is going to Him: Many people were going to Jesus. His growing popularity made some of John’s followers jealous.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
John the Baptist spoke because of two concerns: 

• Some people questioned whether his baptism was from God (see John 1:26), and

• his disciples were worried because many people were beginning to follow Jesus instead of John (John 3:26).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
John the Baptist described Jesus as the bridegroom. He described himself as the bridegroom’s friend.

John did not try to bring honor to himself. Instead, he gave honor to Jesus and showed that Jesus is greater than he is.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus came from heaven. Because of this, he alone was able to make the Father known (John 1:18; John 3:13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: God gives the Spirit without limit: The Father shows his deep love for the Son (John 3:35). This also shows the divine nature of Jesus. John presents the one God as three persons (compare 1 John 5:5–12).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• God gives the gift of eternal life. This life is not only about the future. It begins now. It is a new life and a close relationship with God in the present.

• Whoever rejects the Son will not see life: The world, living in darkness and sin, already stands under God’s judgment (Romans 1–3). This judgment shows God’s anger against sin and evil.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• At an ancient well in Samaria, Jesus offered himself as living water. This living water means the life that comes from God. Jesus spoke openly about who he was. When he revealed God’s truth, people had to respond. They either followed him or turned away.

• The Samaritan woman is very different from Nicodemus. She was a woman, not a man. She was a Samaritan, not a Jew. She had a sinful past, not a reputation for righteousness. She was an outsider, not a respected teacher of Israel.

Nicodemus came to Jesus at night and did not openly respond to the challenges from Jesus (John 3:1–21). The Samaritan woman spoke with Jesus in the daylight. She recognized him as Lord. She remained in the light and showed signs of becoming a disciple (see John 1:35–51).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus himself did not baptize anyone with water. He allowed his disciples to perform water baptism.

Later, after he was lifted up on the cross and then raised from the dead, Jesus returned to the Father. This suffering, death, resurrection, and return to the Father is called his glorification (John 7:37–39). After this, Jesus baptized people in the Holy Spirit (John 1:33; Acts 2:4).

entries.title: John
entries.content: After John the Baptist had been imprisoned, Jesus left Judea (see Mark 6:14–29; compare Mark 1:14).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• When traveling north to Galilee, Jesus chose the less common route through Samaria. Samaria and Judea had a long history of racial tension (see 2 Kings 17:24–41; Ezra 4:1–5; Nehemiah 4; Nehemiah 6:1–19). In the time of Jesus, there was intense racial and cultural conflict between Jews and Samaritans. Jews usually avoided Samaria by first going east to Jericho and then traveling north through the Jordan Valley. 

• Sychar was likely in the area of Shechem. Jesus arrived at Jacob's well. Jacob had owned land near Shechem (Genesis 33:18–19).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Due to the heat, it was customary for the women to draw water in early morning or evening. However, this woman lived in isolation, separated from her community. Jesus was compassionate toward outcasts.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The woman was surprised. Social taboos (strict cultural rules about proper behavior) would normally prevent a Jewish teacher like Jesus from speaking to her (John 4:18). But Jesus did not allow these social rules to control him. He chose to speak with her and offer what she truly needed.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Shechem had no rivers. So it had no living water, which usually means fresh, flowing water from a stream or spring (see “Living Water” Theme Note). However, Jesus was speaking symbolically. The gift he offered was not ordinary water. It was the Holy Spirit, whom God would give to believers (John 7:37–39).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jacob’s well was more than 30 meters (about 100 feet) deep. A person needed a long rope and a container to draw water from it.

The woman focused on the physical water in the well. She did not yet understand the deeper meaning of what Jesus was saying. At that time, she was still in spiritual darkness.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Our father Jacob: The Samaritan woman respected the holy traditions related to the well more than the presence of God in front of her.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
In the dry climate of Israel, a fresh, bubbling spring was a strong and hopeful image. Flowing water meant life, safety, and relief from thirst.

The prophets used this image to describe God’s care. They said that those who come to God will not hunger or thirst (see Isaiah 49:10; Isaiah 55:1–3; Jeremiah 2:13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The woman asked Jesus for this water, but she did not understand the spiritual meaning of his words. To overcome this spiritual barrier, Jesus spoke about her sin (John 4:16–18).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The woman’s immoral life affected her understanding. Her pattern of broken relationships kept her from seeing clearly.

She had been married five times. She was also living with a man who was not her husband. These facts show that her life did not match God’s will. Her sin created a barrier between her and a full understanding of what Jesus was saying.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• a prophet: Jesus revealed knowledge about the woman that a stranger could not know (John 4:16–18; compare John 1:48). 

• As the woman learned more about Jesus, what she called him showed her increasing understanding:

• At first, she recognized him as "a Jew" (John 4:9) and called him "Sir" (John 4:11, John 4:15, John 4:19). 

• Later, she thought he might be "the Christ" (John 4:29), that is, the Messiah (God's chosen one). 

• Finally, the people of the village recognized him as "the Savior of the world" (John 4:42). 

Her growing understanding of the identity of Jesus is a lesson for John’s audience (see John 20:31).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The woman did not answer the moral questions that Jesus asked her. Instead, she changed the subject.

She began to speak about the long-standing division between Jews and Samaritans. This conflict included differences about worship and history. By raising this issue, she moved the conversation away from her personal life.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim. This mountain rises above the city of Shechem.

Both Mount Gerizim and Shechem were important places in the Old Testament (see Genesis 12:6–7; Genesis 33:19; Deuteronomy 11:29; Joshua 8:33; Joshua 24:1, Joshua 24:25, Joshua 24:32).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus affirmed that the Jews had preserved the correct understanding of the one true God whom they worshiped.

• God chose the Jewish people for a special relationship with himself. He gave them his law, his promises, and his covenant (promises between God and his people). The Messiah (God’s chosen one) was to come from the Jewish people (see also Romans 9:4–5).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
in spirit and in truth: In Greek, one preposition (a connecting word) is used for both words. This shows that spirit and truth form one united idea.

True worship happens when God’s Spirit makes God’s truth known to a person. Worship is not only about a place or a ceremony. It is about responding to God with the help of his Spirit and according to what is true about him.

Jesus himself is the Truth (John 14:6). The Spirit is also called the Spirit of truth (John 14:17; John 15:26). Together, the Spirit and the Truth make true worship possible.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
I who speak to you am He: Jesus used an unusual and strong form of the words I am.

This wording may point beyond a simple statement of identity. It can suggest a connection with the name of God revealed in the Old Testament (see John 8:58; Exodus 3:14).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The woman was not fully certain about who Jesus was (John 4:29). She asked the people of her village, “Could this be the Christ?” Her words show that she was still thinking and learning.

Even so, she ran back to the village and told others about him. She invited them to come and see for themselves.

Telling others about Jesus is a sign of discipleship. Earlier in this Gospel, others also invited people to “come and see”(see John 1:39, John 1:46).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
While Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman, the disciples had gone to buy food (John 4:8). When they returned, they urged Jesus to eat. Jesus spoke with symbolic language, but they did not understand him (John 4:33). 

Later, when the disciples received the Holy Spirit, they understood what he meant (John 2:22). Jesus sustained himself spiritually by doing what his Father told him to do (see John 5:30; John 6:38; John 7:18; John 8:50; John 9:4; John 10:37–38; John 12:49–50).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
four months until the harvest: Jesus referred to a common saying about farming. Farmers usually waited about four months between planting seed and gathering the crop.

In Samaria, it was likely the time of harvest, and the fields were ready to be gathered. Jesus used this picture to speak about people, not crops.

He had spoken with the woman at the well and planted spiritual seed (God’s message). Soon after, many Samaritans believed in him (John 4:39–42). In this way, Jesus was already gathering a harvest of faith.

entries.title: John
entries.content: others: Jesus might have meant John the Baptist. Or, he might have been referring to the work he had just done with the Samaritan woman.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Many of the Samaritans: The religious leaders and teachers in Jerusalem did not respond to Jesus with faith (chapter John 3:3). In contrast, many Samaritans believed in him. They first listened because of the testimony (public witness) of this woman, who had been an outsider in her community. Later, they believed because they heard Jesus for themselves.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Samaritans had heard Jesus and believed his message for themselves. They were no longer depending only on the woman’s testimony.

They called him Savior of the world (see also 1 John 4:14). This title shows that they understood something important. Salvation was not limited to one ethnic group.

As Samaritans, they knew they were separated from the Jews. Yet they recognized that Jesus came for all people. His mission was not only for Jews, but for the whole world (John 1:4–12; compare John 12:20–26).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Unlike many people in Jerusalem, the Galileans welcomed Jesus when he came to them.

However, their welcome was based on amazement at his miracles (see John 2:23–25). They were impressed by what he did.

This response was not yet true faith. True faith trusts in who Jesus is, not only in the signs and wonders he performs.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus strongly criticized the Galileans for asking to see miracles and wonders before they would believe (see John 6:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content: "Your son will live": Jesus also healed the centurion’s servant and the Phoenician woman’s daughter from a distance (Matthew 8:5–13; Matthew 15:21–28).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Like many other people, the Jewish official and his household believed in Jesus because of the miracle (John 2:23; John 4:39).

entries.title: John
entries.content: the second sign … in Galilee: Two miracles at Cana frame for this section of John's Gospel (John 2:11; John 4:46). The first miracle was when Jesus turned water into wine. The second was when he healed the official’s son. These two events mark the beginning and the end of this part of the story.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
a feast of the Jews: Jesus returned to Jerusalem for this celebration. Because of this, it was likely one of the three main pilgrimage festivals (special festivals when people traveled to Jerusalem).

In the Old Testament, God commanded Israel to celebrate three such festivals each year (see Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). These were the Feast of Unleavened Bread (also called Passover), the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles.

Each of these festivals lasted about one week. During that time, many people gathered in Jerusalem to worship God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: This chapter is structured like a courtroom case (a legal trial). It begins with a description of the event that led to the conflict (John 5:1–15). This is followed by the decision of the Jewish leaders to take action against Jesus (John 5:16). Next comes a statement of the charges against him (John 5:18). The chapter then presents the defense given by Jesus, where he explains his authority and his relationship with the Father (John 5:17, John 5:19–40).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
In this section, Jesus attends several Jewish feasts and uses their imagery to reveal deeper truths about himself. 

He appears at:

• a Sabbath feast (chapter John 5:5),

• Passover (chapter John 6:6),

• the Feast of Tabernacles (chapters John 7:7–9), and

• the Feast of Dedication (also called Hanukkah; chapter John 10:10). 

In each case, Jesus himself replaces an important element in the ceremonies of the feast.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Greek copyists who had never been to Jerusalem had difficulty interpreting and spelling the name Bethesda, so there are several variants of this name in the manuscripts. The best choice is Beth-esda, which means “house of flowing.”

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The pool of Bethesda was a place for healing where many sick people gathered. They hoped God would cure them with a miracle. 

• Some later manuscripts include an additional verse, John 5:4, which explains that an angel stirred the water. This verse is not included in the Berean Standard Bible because it does not appear in the earliest manuscripts of the Gospel of John. The added verse reflects an early tradition that helps explain why people gathered at the pool.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
No organized care system existed to help this man. He had been sick for 38 years.

He likely could not keep himself clean. He probably could not move easily on his own. Most likely, he depended on begging from people who came to the pool (see John 5:7). From a human point of view, his situation seemed hopeless.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus healed the sick man immediately and only asked him to obey. To prove that the man was healed, Jesus told him to pick up his mat and walk.

• Jesus performed this miracle on the Sabbath. The Sabbath was a weekly day of rest. The law of Moses said that no work should be done on that day (based on Genesis 2:2; Exodus 20:8). Jewish tradition identified 39 types of work that were not allowed (Mishnah Shabbat John 7:2). One rule said that a person could not carry an object, such as a sleeping mat, from one place to another (John 5:10). 

Jesus told the healed man to pick up his mat and walk. When the man obeyed Jesus, he broke this later Jewish tradition.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Who is this man who told you: The focus of the story now changes. It moves from the joy of a miracle to an accusation about breaking the Sabbath.

The religious leaders wanted to know who told the man to carry his mat. They asked for the name of the healer who had broken their tradition.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Stop sinning: Although Jesus healed this man physically, the man still needed to learn to obey the Lord. The man's next action (John 5:15) might indicate that he did not listen.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
My Father is at His work, and I too am working: The Sabbath was a day of rest. People were not supposed to work.

However, Jewish teachers agreed that God still worked on the Sabbath. God gives life through birth. God also takes life in death. God’s work does not stop.

Jesus used this idea to explain his actions. He said that, like his Father, he was also working. By speaking this way, Jesus compared himself with God.

The Jewish leaders understood what he meant. They objected because they believed he was claiming a special right that belongs only to God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus claimed that his work on the Sabbath was the same as God’s work on the Sabbath. Jesus claimed to be equal with God, doing the things God does. Yet he submitted to God’s will, doing only what the Father wanted.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Most Jews firmly believed in resurrection but viewed it as something God alone could accomplish. Jesus claimed that he gives life.

entries.title: John
entries.content: In addition to giving life, Jesus claimed the absolute authority to judge, which belongs to God alone.

entries.title: John
entries.content: the Father who sent Him: In the ancient world, a person could send an authorized representative to seal a contract or make an authoritative decision. Jesus claimed to be God’s representative, so obeying Jesus is the same as obeying God, and dishonoring him is dishonoring God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus is the giver of life as well as the judge (see John 5:21–22), but he never works independently of the Father.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
God's law requires more than one witness in a trial (Deuteronomy 17:6). A single person’s word is not enough to prove a case.

Jesus recognized this principle. He said that his own testimony needed support from others.

So he presented several witnesses who confirmed who he was. These witnesses supported his claims and showed that his message was true.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The first witness who spoke in support of Jesus was God himself.

Jesus may have been thinking about the voice from heaven at his baptism, when God said that Jesus was his Son (Mark 1:11). He may also have meant the power of God that worked through him in his miracles.

In both ways, God gave testimony about who Jesus is.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The second witness of Jesus was John the Baptist. John pointed to Jesus and said that he is the Messiah (John 1:29–34).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The third witness of Jesus was his teachings and miracles. These were signs that revealed his true identity and indicated that the Father sent him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The fourth witness of Jesus was the Scriptures. The Old Testament pointed to the Messiah, and Jesus fulfilled its prophecies (see Luke 24:25–27).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jewish trials were meant to discover the truth. The goal was to decide whether the charges were true or false.

If people were falsely accused, they could show that they were innocent. He could also bring charges against those who had accused him. In this situation, Jesus did that.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus said that the Jewish leaders did not have God’s love in them. They did not truly love God.

Because they did not love God, they could not understand what Jesus was doing. Without love for God, they were unable to recognize God’s work in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Jewish leaders wanted honor and praise from one another. They cared about their reputation and status.

They loved religious activity, but they did not truly love God. Their actions did not match their claims. Because of this, God would judge them (John 5:45–46).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The fifth and final witness for Jesus was Moses, the central figure through whom God gave the law to Israel. Earlier in the Gospel of John, Jesus is compared with Moses, who gave the law, while Jesus brought grace and truth (John 1:17; see also John 6:14–15). The Jewish leaders failed to accept the words of Moses, who spoke clearly about the coming Messiah, including the promise of a prophet like himself (for example, Deuteronomy 18:15).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus feeding the 5,000 recalls the Old Testament story of manna (bread from heaven) when Israel was in the wilderness (Exodus 16). In that story, God provided bread each day for his people.

In the time of Jesus, some Jewish teachers believed that the Messiah would again give bread from heaven (Exodus 16:4). They expected a new act of divine provision.

When Jesus fed the crowd, he met this expectation. However, he was not only giving physical bread. He was pointing to himself as the true bread from heaven, who gives life to the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Each story in this chapter uses the setting of the Feast of the Passover (John 6:4) to communicate a deeper meaning.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Where can we buy bread: When the Israelites left Egypt after the first Passover and entered the desert, finding food and water was also their first concern (Exodus 15:22–16:3).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Barley was a grain for poor people. The loaves were like pita bread. The two fish were likely salted. Together with the five barley loaves, they made one meal.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The count of about 5,000 included only the men, as was the usual way of counting in that culture (Matthew 14:21). Including women and children, the total number of people was much greater.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The simple meal provided the crowd with as much as they wanted. This was similar to the miracle of manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35). In that earlier story, God gave bread from heaven through Moses. Now, Jesus provided bread for the people in a similar way.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world: The crowd understood the miracle as a fulfillment of Old Testament promises (see Deuteronomy 18:15, Deuteronomy 18:18; Malachi 4:5–6).

entries.title: John
entries.content: they were about to come and make Him king by force: To avoid this role, Jesus fled the crowd and commanded his disciples to go back across the lake (Mark 6:45–46).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Strong east-west winds often blow down from the eastern cliffs of the Sea of Galilee. These winds usually come late in the day.

When the wind rushes down toward the water, it can quickly stir up high waves. As a result, the lake can become very rough and dangerous. Sudden and violent storms were common in that area.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The disciples were afraid of the storm. Then they saw Jesus walking on the water toward them. At that moment, their fear of the storm was replaced by fear and awe of him. Jesus came to help them. By walking on the water, he showed his authority over nature.

This act recalled Moses, who led Israel safely through the water (Exodus 14; see Psalm 77:19–20).

entries.title: John
entries.content: It is I (literally, I am): Jesus identified himself by the name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see Exodus 3:14; also see John 4:26; John 6:35).

entries.title: John
entries.content: at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading: The healing happened at once. This immediate result was another miracle performed by Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The crowd sailed north to Capernaum to search for Jesus because he had made Capernaum his home in Galilee (Mark 2:1).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The crowd had decided that Jesus was a prophet. They even wanted to use him for their own political goals (see John 6:15). 

However, they did not understand the true meaning of the miracle. They focused on the bread and the signs.

Jesus then explained what the miracle really meant. He taught that people should not work only for food that spoils. Instead, they should seek the food that gives eternal life (John 6:27–59).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This dialogue took place in the synagogue at Capernaum shortly before Passover (John 6:4, 59). During Passover, Jews would read the story of the exodus from Egypt (see Exodus 1–15).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The greatest gift Jesus gives is not physical bread, but eternal life. The Father gave Jesus the authority to do this. 

Physical food spoils. But Jesus, who is the bread of life, offers a gift that lasts forever (John 6:35).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The crowd asked Jesus for another miraculous sign. They wanted proof that he was the Messiah.

Many Jews believed that when the Messiah came, he would repeat the great miracle connected with Moses. They expected manna to fall from heaven again, as it had in the wilderness.

If that happened, people would see it as a second exodus. It would remind them of how God rescued Israel from Egypt and fed them in the desert.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus corrected the people's argument: God, not Moses, fed Israel in the wilderness. 

The most important goal in life is to seek the true bread from God. This bread is not ordinary food. It is the gift that gives eternal life. To “eat” this bread means to believe in Jesus and depend on him.

Those who receive this bread share in the life that comes from God and lasts forever.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Sir, … give us this bread: This is similar to the request of the Samaritan woman (John 4:15). Spiritual awakening begins with a request for God’s gift.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In the Gospel of John, the “I am” statements reveal who Jesus is and what he came to do (see also John 4:26; John 8:12; John 9:5; John 10:7–9, John 10:11–14; John 11:25; John 14:6; John 15:1–5). Jesus used the words I am on purpose. These words would remind his listeners of the name of God in the Old Testament (Exodus 3:14). 

• I am the bread of life: Jesus is the true manna that came from God (John 6:38). He satisfies the spiritual hunger of those who believe in him (compare John 4:10–13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Everyone the Father gives Me: God acts to bring people to Jesus so that they believe in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The mission of Jesus is sure to succeed. God sent Jesus and calls people to follow him (John 6:37, 38, 44). Those who come to him are secure in the promise Jesus gave that he will not reject them or lose them (John 6:39).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• When Jesus called himself the bread that came down from heaven, the crowd had to make a decision. 

• Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph: The people questioned Jesus because they thought they knew him and his family.

Their familiarity with him made his claims seem strange and unbelievable. Since they saw him as an ordinary man from their town, they struggled to accept what he said about himself.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Stop grumbling: Instead of defending himself against their complaint, Jesus addresses their lack of spiritual receptivity (their openness to God; see John 6:42). Those who love the Father and listen to him will believe in Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus connected the manna of the exodus story with himself. Then he said why he was different from the manna the Israelites received from God. 

The Israelites remained mortal and they all died. But the bread from heaven (Jesus himself) provides eternal life (John 6:47, John 6:51, John 6:58).

entries.title: John
entries.content: this bread … is My flesh: The gift that gives life is now made clear. On the cross, Jesus gave his body so that the world might receive life.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
eats My flesh and drinks My blood: Jesus answered the question the people asked (John 6:52). His words pointed ahead to the Lord’s Supper, which would come later (see Luke 22:19). In Jewish speech, the phrase “flesh and blood” referred to the whole person. In this context, Jesus was calling people to receive him fully by completely believing in him.

Ever since the Protestant Reformation, there have been three main interpretations of the words of Jesus about the bread and wine: 

• Transubstantiation: The bread and wine are believed to change into the actual body and blood of Christ, while still appearing to be bread and wine.

• Real Presence: Christ is understood to be truly present in the sacrament in a mysterious but real way that is beyond human understanding.

• Memorial or Symbolic View: The bread and wine are seen as symbols. The act of sharing them recalls Christ’s death and resurrection, and believers receive spiritual benefit through faith.

entries.title: John
entries.content: What Jesus said was shocking and offensive (John 6:53–58; see Genesis 9:4–5). It was hard for his disciples and the crowd to understand. Should they take him literally? How could they eat his flesh? Jesus answers in John 6:63.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The true source of the gift Jesus gives is the Holy Spirit, not human effort. In this context, the flesh refers to what humans can do on their own. Life and understanding come through the gift of the Spirit (see John 14:15–20; John 20:21–22). True life is found only when the Holy Spirit gives life to people.

entries.title: John
entries.content: no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him (see John 6:44): Only God’s light can shine into the deep darkness of the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Simon Peter often spoke on behalf of the 12 apostles (see also Matthew 14:28–29; Matthew 16:16; Matthew 17:4; Matthew 18:21; Matthew 19:27; Matthew 26:33–35).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Once again, Jesus showed supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability; see John 1:47–49; John 4:16–19). He knew what was in people’s hearts (their innermost selves) and what would happen in the future.

Jesus knew that Judas would betray him. Judas later betrayed Jesus to the authorities (John 12:4; John 13:2; Matthew 26:14–16). 

• Iscariot means “man from Kerioth.” Kerioth was the home village of Judas’s family.

entries.title: John
entries.content: This chapter describes Jesus at the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus used parts of the feast to reveal his true identity to his fellow Jews and to show that he had fulfilled the feast's essential meaning (see John 7:37–39; John 8:12).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The law of Moses required Jewish men to come to the temple for the Feast of Tabernacles (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). This annual seven-day autumn harvest feast happened in Jerusalem six months after Passover (John 6:4). 

During the feast, people lived in temporary shelters to remember the tents Israel used during their 40 years in the wilderness.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The brothers of Jesus reminded him of his religious duty to go to the festival (see also Mark 3:31). Their words carried a cynical tone because at this time they did not believe in him (John 7:5).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
My time has not yet come: Jesus said that it was not the right time for him to go publicly to Jerusalem.

Later, however, he did go to the city. He went quietly and not in a public way (John 7:10; compare study note on 12:23).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
They wondered how he could teach with such understanding.

Jesus had not studied under a well-known rabbi (a Jewish teacher of the law). Instead, he said that his teaching came from his heavenly Father.

This was different from many Jewish teachers. For example, Peter and John were known as untrained men (Acts 4:13). In contrast, Paul had studied under a respected teacher (Acts 22:3).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
People who truly want to follow God's will accept Jesus and his teachings (see also John 5:42–47). 

In contrast, those who focus only on the values and desires of this world are not open to Christ. When people care more about human approval, power, or temporary success, they struggle to receive his message.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it: The Jewish leaders were proud of the law of Moses. They believed they carefully obeyed it.

However, Jesus pointed out a serious problem. While they honored the law in words, they were planning to kill him. In doing so, they were breaking the law (Exodus 20:13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: You have a demon: See John 8:48–52; John 10:20–21.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The law required circumcision on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). It allowed a boy to be circumcised even if that day was the Sabbath. 

Jesus argued in the way many rabbis did. They reasoned from the lesser to the greater. If a smaller religious act, such as circumcision, was allowed on the Sabbath, then a greater act, such as making a whole person well, should also be allowed.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Some people in the crowd believed they knew where Jesus came from. Because they could trace his earthly origins, they thought he could not be the Messiah.

They expected the Messiah to appear suddenly and in a mysterious way. Since Jesus had grown up among them, they assumed he did not fit their expectations.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
I am from Him: Instead of answering questions about where he grew up (John 7:27, John 7:40–44), Jesus spoke about where he truly came from. He pointed to his heavenly origin.

He said that he was sent by God. This was a bold claim.

The religious leaders understood what he meant. Because of this, they tried to arrest him. They believed he was speaking in a way that dishonored God (John 7:30; compare John 10:30–33).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
His hour had not yet come: Those who opposed Jesus could not arrest him. This was because, according to God's plan, the time for Jesus to be glorified on the cross had not yet come (see study note on 12:23; see also John 10:17–18; John 18:6–8). 

All four arrest scenes in John 7:1–8:59 emphasize that Jesus was in control, not the Jewish leaders.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus announced his return to the one who sent him, the Father in heaven (John 17:1–7). But the Pharisees misunderstood him. They thought he was leaving Judea to visit the Gentiles (non-Jewish people). These were people whom Pharisees would never visit. 

• After Jesus returned to the Father, the Jewish leaders would no longer be able to find him.

• and where I am, you cannot come: These Pharisees, still in spiritual darkness, could not enter heaven. So Jesus would be beyond their reach there.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Living water: See John 4:10–14. A water ceremony was held each day during the Feast of Tabernacles, with prayer for God to send rain in the late autumn. 

The final day, called the great day, was the feast's most important moment. On this day, they repeated the ceremony seven times. They poured water over the altar while Levites sang Isaiah 12:3 (see Zechariah 14:8; see also Mishnah Sukkah chapter 4). 

• If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink: Jesus fulfilled an important part of the Feast of Tabernacles. He himself is the source of living water, available to anyone who believes.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
In the death and resurrection of Jesus, his life was given for others, and the Holy Spirit was given to believers.

When Jesus was crucified, blood and water flowed from his side (see John 19:34). This event points to the gift of life that comes through his death.

After he rose from the dead, he breathed on his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). In this way, his life and the Spirit were poured out for his followers.

entries.title: John
entries.content: These Jews were not like the crowd who thought the Christ (the Messiah) would have a mysterious appearance (John 7:25–27). They believed the prophecy that God's chosen ruler would come from Bethlehem in Judea (see Micah 5:2). However, they struggled with the fact that Jesus seemed to be from Galilee, where he grew up.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The story ends with Jewish leaders feeling frustrated and the people being divided over their opinion of Jesus (compare John 7:25–27, John 7:31–32). 

• officers returned: See John 7:32.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Nicodemus was likely starting to believe in Jesus (see John 3:1–21; John 19:38–42). Some leaders claimed that none of the Pharisees believed in Jesus (John 7:48). They spoke as if only the crowd, whom the leaders believed did not understand the law, supported him.

However, Nicodemus shows that this was not completely true. Not only the people in the crowd, but also some Pharisees were beginning to believe in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: no prophet comes out of Galilee: The Jewish leaders were apparently unaware that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, not in Galilee (see Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:1–7).

entries.title: John
entries.content: It is likely that someone added this story to John's Gospel later, since it is not in the earliest Greek manuscripts. However, it is likely a true story from the life of Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The scribes and Pharisees: The teachers of religious law were Jewish scholars. They specialized in the Old Testament law and oral traditions that explained it.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The form of the Greek sentence emphasizes the legal claim against the woman. She had been caught while committing the sin of adultery. The law required two witnesses and carefully outlined what evidence was needed.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In the Law Moses commanded us to stone: This suggests the woman was engaged or married (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:23–24). The law also indicates that the man who sinned with her must die as well. But these Jewish religious leaders ignored that part of the law. 

• They could have dealt with the situation privately to avoid shaming her. But their real intention was to condemn Jesus instead. They asked him, So what do you say? 

Would he neglect the law since he had a reputation for mercy? Or would he ignore the woman’s tragedy?

entries.title: John
entries.content: We cannot know what Jesus wrote in the dust. Some scholars suggest he wrote down the sins of those who were accusing the woman.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The answer Jesus gave did not mean that someone who makes an accusation must be morally perfect to make legal claims. He referred to him who is without sin to point to the motives of those accusing her.

entries.title: John
entries.content: they began to go away one by one: One of the people accusing her left, then another, followed by several people who had been standing there watching what was happening.

entries.title: John
entries.content: neither do I: Jesus spoke words of assurance, but this did not suggest that the woman was innocent. Jesus takes sin and judgment seriously, but he shows grace and forgiveness to those overcome by sin.

entries.title: John
entries.content: During the Festival of Tabernacles, people filled 16 gold bowls in the temple's inner courts with oil and lit them. Jesus stood under these lights in the temple and said that he was now the source of the light of the world (John 8:20). The light of Jesus brings salvation to both Israel and the world, regardless of race or location.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The debate about whether Jesus is the Messiah continues from John 7:52. Jesus remained at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. During the feast, the conflicts Jesus encountered in chapter John 7:7 continued and intensified.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Pharisees argued that what Jesus was saying about himself was not valid because Jewish law requires more than one witness (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare John 5:31–32; see John 8:17).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus responded to the Pharisees' accusations. He said he could make these claims about himself because he knew both his origin and his destination were heaven. He then said the most important witness for his case was his Father who sent him (John 8:16).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Throughout the feast, those listening to Jesus proved they were in darkness as they misunderstood him. They wanted to meet the father of Jesus, who is God. Since they did not truly know God, they were unable to understand Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The treasury was in the section of the temple called the Court of the Women. Jesus often taught there so both men and women could listen (Mark 12:41). 

• His hour: See notes on John 2:4; John 12:23.

entries.title: John
entries.content: In the earlier debate at the feast, people questioned where Jesus came from (John 7:27). Here, Jesus talked about returning to where he came from (heaven). However, once again, his words were misunderstood by the people listening.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus told his listeners that they were from below, while he was from above (John 3:31; see study note on 3:3).

From below refers to human life limited to this world. From above refers to heaven and to God’s realm.

Because they were thinking only in earthly terms, they could not understand what Jesus meant. His origin and authority came from God.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• unless you believe that I am He: Jesus used God's divine name (see John 4:26; Exodus 3:14). His listeners did not fully understand the meaning of his words (John 8:25). 

• die in your sins: Jesus is the light who has come into the world. His presence offers the only way of salvation. If people reject him, they remain in darkness and do not receive life.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Who are you?: Later, they understood what he was claiming about himself. They believed he was showing dishonor toward God. Because of this, they tried to stone him (John 8:59).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus as predicting his death three times (for example, Mark 8:31; Mark 9:31; Mark 10:33–34). 

The Gospel of John presents this theme in a different way. Jesus speaks about being lifted up (John 3:14; John 8:28; John 12:33–34). This phrase refers to his crucifixion and also to his glory. The Father directs the course of events. The death of Jesus did not happen by accident, but according to God’s plan.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Once again, the crowd at the feast was divided. Earlier, the discussion had ended with plans to arrest Jesus (John 8:20). Now many people believed in him. They were persuaded that he was speaking the truth.

However, when Jesus spoke more clearly about who he really was, their faith was tested. As his full identity became known, some struggled to accept his words (John 8:31–59).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Discipleship involves more than just knowing who Jesus is. It also requires obeying his teachings (John 3:36; John 14:15, John 14:21, John 14:23; John 15:10). 

• Because Jesus is the truth, knowing him helps a person understand what is true and what is false (John 14:6).

• set you free: The truth frees a person from darkness, lies, and sin.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus challenged a common belief about Israel as God’s chosen people. Many thought that being descendants of Abraham gave them special privilege and protection.

Instead of seeing this heritage as a responsibility to obey God, some treated it as a guarantee of safety. However, the prophets had warned that privilege brings accountability (compare Amos 3:1–15). 

• The people did not understand what Jesus meant by set free. He was not talking about freedom from human slavery. He meant freedom from spiritual slavery to sin (John 8:34). 

True freedom comes through the truth. It does not come from family history or religious background (John 8:32; Romans 6:17; Romans 8:2; 1 John 3:4, 1 John 3:8, 1 John 3:9).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus explained his argument: If Israel is a spiritual slave, it has the same insecurity as any slave in a household. Family members are secure, but slaves are not. Only Jesus can change the status of those in spiritual slavery, making them free and secure.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The leaders' plan to kill Jesus revealed their true identity (John 5:18). They were part of a different spiritual family, and their spiritual father was not Jesus's Father. They were relying on the fact that their ancestral father was Abraham, but Jesus challenged their spiritual heritage. 

The most important part of his challenge comes in John 8:44.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• your father: Jesus knew who controlled them. 

• We are not illegitimate children: This statement acted as both a defense and an attack. The Greek text emphasizes the pronoun we. In other words, “We [in contrast to you] are not illegitimate.” They are suggesting that Jesus was illegitimate (see Matthew 1:18–25).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Since the unbelieving people did not love Jesus (John 8:42; 1 John 5:1), they were not children of the Father in heaven who sent his beloved Son (John 8:47). Their desire to kill God’s Son showed their true spiritual heritage. This was the work of the devil, who brought death to the world (see Genesis 3:1–20; Romans 5:12–14).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
By calling Jesus a Samaritan with a demon, his opponents used a racial insult to dismiss his accusations (see study note on 4:4–6). They claimed Jesus was demon-possessed to counter his claim that they belonged to Satan (also John 7:20; John 8:52; John 10:20; John 8:44). 

Jesus rightly replied that these words were deeply offensive. In fact, it was a serious and unforgivable offense (Mark 3:22–29).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Who do You claim to be?: This question was hostile and aggressive. However, if Jesus is immortal, ruling over life and death, then he is greater than Abraham, the prophets, or any of the greatest people in Israel’s history (John 8:58).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Like his opponents, Jesus appealed to Abraham. Rabbis taught that God had given Abraham prophetic insight, teaching him about the coming age of the Messiah.

entries.title: John
entries.content: You are not yet fifty years old: The Jewish leaders misunderstood Jesus. Jesus was not talking about his physical age. He was speaking about his divine pre-existence (his existence before he was born as a human).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• before Abraham was born, I am!: The life of Jesus spans the past from before creation and continues forever (John 1:1–2). 

• I am: This title recalls the name of God revealed to Moses at Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:14; compare John 4:26; Isaiah 43:11–13; Isaiah 48:12).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Those listening to Jesus finally understood his claim to be God (John 8:58). Because of this, they became very angry. They believed they had heard blasphemy (words that dishonored God) and picked up stones to throw at him, which was the proper legal response (Leviticus 24:16). 

• Jesus was hidden from them because God had chosen a different time for his death (see study note on John 12:23; see also John 7:30, John 7:44; Luke 4:29–30).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus claimed to be the light of the world (chapters John 7:7–8; see John 8:12). Now John tells about Jesus giving light, both physically and spiritually, to a blind man who lived in darkness (see John 9:5). 

The story ends with a surprising reversal (a complete change) of roles: The man who had been blind was assumed to live in spiritual darkness. Yet he came to see and accept God’s light. The Pharisees could see with their physical eyes. People thought they were spiritually enlightened (well taught and wise). However, they refused to believe. In the end, they were shown to be spiritually blind.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The disciples thought the man was born blind because of sin, either his own sin or his parents'. Jesus corrected this common belief (John 9:3).

entries.title: John
entries.content: I am the light of the world: See study note on 8:12.

entries.title: John
entries.content: During the New Testament era, saliva was used for medical purposes (see Mark 7:32–35; Mark 8:22–25).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Siloam, a pool at the south end of Jerusalem, provided water for the Feast of Tabernacles ceremonies. 

• which means “Sent”: This phrase contained a double meaning: Jesus, who has been sent by God, told the blind man to wash in the pool called Sent (John 4:34; John 5:23, John 5:37; John 7:28; John 8:26; John 12:44; John 14:24).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The blind man recognized Jesus and spoke with confidence about him. Jesus healed the man of his physical problem, and the man gained more spiritual understanding (John 9:17, John 9:33). He became a disciple of Jesus (John 9:38; compare John 5:11–15).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Pharisees were experts in interpreting the Jewish law. So the community asked them to explain this miracle (see John 1:24). Instead of celebrating the healing, these religious leaders questioned the man because Jesus had performed the miracle on the Sabbath (see John 5:16–18).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The man had already identified his healer (John 9:11, John 9:16). Now he made his own spiritual judgment, calling Jesus a prophet.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Pharisees wanted to dismiss the miracle. They did not want to accept that Jesus had truly healed the man.

They called the man’s parents and questioned them. They hoped the parents would deny that a real healing had taken place.

entries.title: John
entries.content: His parents confirmed that their son had been born blind, but they hesitated to judge how he could see because they were afraid of the social consequences.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Give glory to God!: Compare Joshua 7:19.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The Pharisees could not argue against the logic of the miracle (John 9:24–25, John 9:30–33). So they abandoned reason and cursed him (see John 9:34). 

• The harsh division between Jesus and the religious leaders was clear. They considered those who followed Jesus to have rejected Moses and Judaism.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Jewish leaders did not know where Jesus came from. It made sense that the man was amazed. A healing like this had never happened before. 

The work of Jesus showed he was from God. Once people knew who he truly was, they should have believed and followed him. However, the Jewish leaders chose to ignore the truth.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Only God could give sight to someone born blind. By healing the man, Jesus gave the Jewish leaders an obvious sign that he was from God and was the Messiah (compare Psalm 146:8; Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 42:7).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Discipline such as being thrown out of the synagogue was not uncommon. It brought social isolation that might require the man’s departure from the village. Such serious persecution was precisely what Jesus predicted for his followers (John 15:18–27; John 16:2).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Son of Man: See John 1:51; John 3:13, John 3:14; John 5:27; John 6:27, John 6:53, John 6:62; John 8:28. The Greek expression translates a Hebrew and Aramaic phrase that means human being. People were often unsure what Jesus meant when he used this title (see John 12:34). In Daniel 7:13–14, a human figure receives authority and an eternal kingdom from God. Later Jewish tradition connected this figure with hopes for the Messiah. John uses the title Son of Man to point to Jesus as both an ordinary human being and the Messiah appointed by God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus urged the man who had been blind to understand the miracle and recognize the one who healed him. The man immediately showed faith and honored Jesus in the same way he would honor God (John 9:38; compare John 20:28).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Are we blind too?: Jesus answered that those who claim to hold all religious truth will discover that they are blind, while those who recognize their spiritual poverty will find true sight. In the story, the blind man and his family frequently confessed that they did not know, while the Pharisees repeatedly stated their confidence and remained guilty because of their religious pride. If they had confessed their ignorance and admitted their spiritual blindness, they would be guiltless. Instead, their conscious and willful rejection of Jesus established their guilt.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• A shepherd in the wild would build a sheepfold. This was a pen with low stone walls topped by sharp branches, to keep his sheep safe at night. 

• The pen had one gate (or opening in the wall) that was closed with branches. Any person or thing that came into the pen threatened the flock. 

• A bad shepherd was like a thief and a robber. He used the sheep for his own gain and did not care for them. Bad shepherds took the sheep’s milk and wool for themselves. They killed the sheep without guaranteeing their safety (Ezekiel 34:3; see Isaiah 56:11; Jeremiah 23:1–4). 

These words were the strongest rebuke Jesus spoke against the Jewish leaders.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
This illustration of a shepherd and his sheep comes from a Middle Eastern perspective of shepherding and Old Testament traditions in first-century AD Jewish culture. God was the shepherd of Israel (Genesis 49:24; Psalms 23; Psalms 78:52–53; Isaiah 40:10–11). 

Spiritual and political leaders of Israel were also shepherds of God’s people, the flock of God (Isaiah 56:9–12; Jeremiah 23:1–4; Ezekiel 34). 

Jesus spoke these words during the Feast of Dedication (see John 10:22). At that time, people remembered both faithful and unfaithful leaders in Israel’s history.

In this setting, Jesus addressed the theme of shepherds. He spoke in a way that echoes Ezekiel 34, where God condemns bad shepherds and promises to care for his people himself. Jesus then identified himself as the good shepherd (John 10:11–14).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Chapter 10 continues the series of feast sermons (see study note on 5:1–10:42). Here, the setting is the Feast of Dedication. The timing of this feast is important for understanding the story (see study note on 10:22).

entries.title: John
entries.content: the sheep listen for his voice: The Middle Eastern shepherd is well known for having intimate knowledge of the sheep. Sheep are led with flute tunes, songs, or verbal commands.

entries.title: John
entries.content: A good shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and leads them. He does not force them from behind. When the sheep recognize his voice, they trust him and follow.
