entries.title: John
entries.content: I am: See study note on 6:35. A good shepherd protects the sheep at the gate like a guard.

entries.title: John
entries.content: he will be saved (or will find safety): As the guard at the gate, Jesus protects his sheep from harm by keeping them safe inside the pen.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The followers of Jesus must be wary of bad shepherds who desire to steal and kill and destroy. When they told the story of the Feast of Dedication to the Jewish people, it reminded them of false religious leaders (see study note on 10:22). The failures of these leaders had led to the loss of God's temple in Jerusalem during the time of the Maccabean Revolt.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Small villages often created communal flocks and employed a hired hand to tend the sheep. However, an employee lacked the commitment of a true shepherd. The wilderness of Judea had many predators. When a wolf or other predators attacked, the hired hand would run rather than defend the sheep. Jesus will never do this; he will always stand between his sheep and danger.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
I am: See study note on 6:35. The good shepherd guides his sheep, finds food and water, and locates paths in the wilderness (see Psalm 23). The good shepherd stands between his sheep and danger (John 10:11). 

The Old Testament describes God as Israel’s shepherd (Psalms 23; Psalms 80:1; Isaiah 40:10–11). The religious leaders of God’s people should care for their flock as God does (Ezekiel 34:23). However, the leaders of Israel in the time of Jesus were not good shepherds.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I give my life for the sheep: Jesus was speaking about his coming death. He was referring to his crucifixion (his death on a cross; chapter John 19:19).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Father and the Son have an intimate relationship. Jesus shares a similar relationship with his sheep (his followers) through the Holy Spirit (John 14:23–31; John 15:1–11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: other sheep: Jesus spoke about sheep who were not part of the present sheepfold. This refers to people outside Judaism who would later believe in him (see John 11:52). The followers of Jesus would not be divided by ethnic background. Jewish and Gentile believers from many cultures would become one flock. There would be one shepherd and one united people (John 17:20–23).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• No one takes it from Me: The death of the Son was voluntary. Jesus was not a helpless victim of events beyond his control. He chose to give his life freely in obedience and close relationship with the Father (see Acts 2:23–24). 

• The resurrection of Jesus was not an afterthought or a rescue from failure. God cannot be confined by death or a tomb. Because Jesus and the Father are one, Jesus possessed the authority to rise from death.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus divided his audience yet again (see also John 6:66–69; John 7:43; John 9:16). His words and actions led people to one of two responses: opposition or faith.

• He is demon-possessed: Compare John 7:20; John 8:48–49, John 8:52.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
the Feast of Dedication: This winter feast is also known as Hanukkah. It celebrates the time when the Jews rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV (175–163 BC) defiled it in. Two hundred years before Jesus was born, Greek soldiers captured the Jerusalem Temple, stole its treasures, and made it unusable for worship. 

In the winter of 165–164 BC, a Jewish army led by Judas Maccabeus reclaimed the temple and rededicated it to the Lord. The Feast of Hanukkah ("dedication") celebrates this event (see 1 Maccabees 3–4; 2 Maccabees 8:1–10:8). 

During the feast, priests examined their commitment to service, using Ezekiel 34 as their main text for reflection (also Jeremiah 23:1–4; Jeremiah 25:32–38; Zechariah 11). At this Hanukkah celebration, Jesus used the shepherd theme from Ezekiel 34 to show he was the good shepherd (John 10:11). He also showed how Israel’s current religious leaders were bad shepherds (John 10:10, John 10:12–13).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Large covered walkways with rows of columns stood around all four sides of the temple’s central courtyard. These structures are called colonnades.

Solomon’s Colonnade was on the east side. It provided shelter from wind and rain, especially during the winter months.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The people around Jesus might have been trying to understand, or they might have been hostile. In Luke 21:20 and Hebrews 11:30, the same word describes how armies surrounded Jerusalem and Jericho before their destruction. In Acts 14:20, it refers to Paul's disciples gathering around him after he was injured.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus had already provided the Jewish people and their religious leaders with sufficient proof that he is the Son of God. The problem was not lack of information, but their unwillingness to believe him.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
In his final public statement in this Gospel, Jesus gave a clear and complete declaration about who he is (John 10:30). He spoke openly about his unity with the Father.

This statement brought his public teaching to a high point and made his identity unmistakable.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• As the good shepherd, Jesus would die for his sheep and protect them from all predators and thieves (John 10:1, John 10:8, John 10:11; see Ezekiel 34:22–23). 

• The Father's power, shown through Jesus, keeps his sheep safe. No one can steal from Jesus those who trust in him. This is because no one is stronger than Jesus. Their security depends on Christ, not their own efforts. 

• The word translated as snatch suggests violence (as in John 6:15).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Father and the Son are distinct persons, yet they share one purpose and one divine nature (John 1:1, John 1:14; John 14:9; John 20:28). They are not the same person. Yet they are united in will, authority, and being.

Because of this unity, Jesus has the power to protect God’s flock (John 10:28–29). His words are a strong statement about his divinity.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The people understood what Jesus meant and wanted to kill him (see John 10:33). The problem was not that Jesus performed good works, but that he claimed to be God (see John 6:42, John 6:60; John 7:29–30). Blasphemy (speaking in a way that dishonors God) was punishable by death under the law of Moses. The required punishment was stoning (see Leviticus 24:23; John 8:59).

entries.title: John
entries.content: ‘I have said you are gods’: If the word gods could describe people other than the Lord, then Jesus was not breaking the law by referring to himself in this way. But Jesus is not just any son of God. Jesus is the Son of God who the Father sent into the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The miraculous works Jesus performed should help true believers know and understand that the full reality of God dwells in Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content: His revelation to the Jewish leaders now complete, Jesus went to the region beyond the Jordan River where John the Baptist had once worked and where Jesus was baptized.

entries.title: John
entries.content: everything he said about this man was true: See John 1:19–51; John 3:22–36. The fulfillment of John the Baptist’s predictions confirms both that he was a prophet and that what he said about Jesus was true.

entries.title: John
entries.content: This is a note of irony (an unexpected contrast). In Jerusalem, the holy city, Jesus found little faith among the religious leaders. But in the desert, away from the center of religious power, many people believed in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In the Hebrew language, Lazarus is a shortened form of Eleazar, which means "God helps." In the first century, it was the fourth most common name for Jewish men (see also Luke 16:19–31). 

• Bethany was a small village east of Jerusalem, just past the Mount of Olives (John 11:18). Jesus often stayed there when he visited Jerusalem. He likely traveled through Bethany on his way to Jerusalem. This was because most Jews from Galilee took a route going south to Jericho, then west to Jerusalem. 

• Mary and Martha were sisters (see Luke 10:38–42). Martha was probably older. She was the host in Luke’s Gospel and represented the family. Mary later anointed Jesus with perfume (John 12:1–8).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The resurrection of Lazarus points to the future death and resurrection of Jesus. The description of Lazarus’s tomb is similar to the description of the tomb Jesus was placed in after he died (John 11:38, John 11:44; John 20:1, John 20:7). Both accounts mention a cave and burial cloths. These details connect the two events and help us see that Lazarus’s story is a sign.

Soon after Lazarus was raised, a woman anointed Jesus for burial (John 12:3). This act prepared him for his coming death.

Then the time for his glorification began (John 12:23).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The two sisters had a difficult choice to make. They knew Jesus was able to heal, but they also realized that his return to Judea would involve personal risk (John 11:8).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus responded with words that were similar to his words about the man born blind (John 9:1–5). Jesus already knew Lazarus was dead (John 11:14). He was talking about Lazarus's resurrection, which would bring glory to God (John 11:43).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The trip to Bethany from where Jesus was staying would have taken only one day (see John 10:40). However, Jesus followed his own timing and did not let others rush him (John 2:4; John 7:5–9).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The disciples were rightly worried about the risk (see John 7:25; John 8:37, John 8:44, John 8:59; John 10:31, John 10:39).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Thomas: See also John 14:5; John 20:24; John 21:2; Mark 3:18. 

• Let us also go, so that we may die: Thomas knew that earlier visits to Judea had been risky (John 5:18; John 10:31, John 10:39). Traveling to Jerusalem now would likely mean death for Jesus (compare John 11:49–50).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
In Jewish custom at that time, people were usually buried on the same day they died. Families placed the body in a tomb quickly, often within hours.

John tells us that Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days. This detail is important. It shows that Lazarus was truly dead.

Because four days had passed, this miracle was not a simple resuscitation (bringing someone back who only seemed dead). Jesus did not restore a weak person who might recover. He raised a man who had been dead and buried for several days.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Life in New Testament times was lived publicly. Lazarus’s large extended family, as well as the villagers, had arrived for a seven-day mourning period. To console the sisters in their loss, there was great wailing and crying (see John 11:33 and corresponding study note).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Lord, if You had been here: Mary later repeated Martha’s words (John 11:32), because both sisters knew that Jesus had a reputation as a healer. They concluded that Jesus would have healed Lazarus, but they did not imagine that Jesus would restore him from death.

entries.title: John
entries.content: whatever You ask of Him: Martha believed Jesus could still help in some way. Despite this, she objected when Jesus wanted to open the tomb (John 11:39). She did not think Jesus would resurrect her brother from the dead.

entries.title: John
entries.content: rise again in the resurrection at the last day: Martha misunderstood Jesus because she thought he meant the general resurrection of all dead people at the end of time (compare John 11:11–13).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus helped Martha believe in him not only as someone who heals, but as someone who defeats death. 

• I am the resurrection and the life: Victory over death comes from living in union with Jesus. Although the followers of Jesus will one day die, they will have eternal life after death. For more on the I am statements of Jesus, see the study note on 6:35.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Do you believe this?: Jesus was not simply asking Martha if he could bring Lazarus out of the grave. Martha already believed that Lazarus would rise again on the last day.

Instead, Jesus asked a deeper question. Did Martha believe that life itself is connected to him?

• “Yes, Lord”: Even though she did not fully understand, she acknowledged that Jesus was the Christ, God's chosen one. But she was still surprised by his power.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Mary now joined the scene on the edge of the village, repeating her sister’s cry of misery. She fell at the feet of Jesus, not in worship but in desperate grief.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Loud weeping and crying out were common public displays of grief in this culture, as was beating one's chest (Mark 5:38; Luke 18:13). 

• The Greek word translated deeply moved in spirit describes strong human emotion, including outrage or anger. Jesus was not angry at Martha or Mary. Jesus was angry because the situation showed the people’s lack of belief, even though resurrection was real and near.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Lazarus was buried in a tomb cut from the rocky hillside; such tombs were common. The tomb was closed and opened for further burials with a rolling stone that covered the entrance. A central door led to a cave room where burial benches were carved in stone along the inner wall. Horizontal burial chambers were cut along the top edge of the benches.

entries.title: John
entries.content: News of the miracle quickly spread to Jerusalem (John 12:9, John 12:17). Again, people had different opinions about who Jesus was (John 6:66–69; John 7:43; John 9:16; John 10:19; John 11:37). Jesus was famous in Galilee for healing and raising the dead (see Matthew 9:24–26; Matthew 10:8; Matthew 11:5). Now he had brought this power to Judea.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The council met to discuss what to do about Jesus. During their discussion, they revealed their fear. They were afraid that everyone would believe in him.

If many people believed that Jesus was the Messiah (God’s chosen one), this could cause political trouble. In that time, the Romans ruled over Judea. They did not tolerate leaders who claimed to be kings.

The Romans viewed Jewish messiahs with suspicion. They feared rebellion. The council worried that the growing movement around Jesus might lead the Romans to attack Jerusalem and destroy the temple.

So their concern was not only religious. It was also political. They feared losing their place, their authority, and even their nation.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Caiaphas was the ruler of the high council from AD 18–36. He worked for ten years alongside Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea (AD 26–36; see John 18:29), keeping the peace with Rome.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
it is better … that one man die: Caiaphas spoke with clear political intent. He argued that it was better for one man to die than for the whole nation to suffer. He meant that it was better for Jesus, whom he saw as a threat, to die than for Rome to destroy the Jewish people.

Caiaphas viewed Jesus as a possible revolutionary. He feared that Rome would crush the nation if unrest grew. From his point of view, sacrificing one man would protect many.

But his words carried a deeper meaning. Caiaphas did not understand this meaning. In a way he could not see, he spoke the truth. Jesus would die for the people. His death would bring salvation (rescue from sin and separation from God).

John explains that Caiaphas did not speak on his own authority. As high priest that year, he spoke prophetically (as one who speaks a message from God). God used his words to point to the saving purpose of the death of Jesus.

The rescue that God’s people needed was not mainly from Rome. It would come through the cross of Christ.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Christ’s death was not for Israel only, but for all, including people of other cultures all across the world (John 10:16; John 12:32).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• When the Jewish leaders started planning to kill Jesus, Jesus responded carefully (John 11:54). He did not act in fear, but he acted wisely. He chose to leave the area for a time.

• Ephraim was a village about 19 kilometers (12 miles) north of Jerusalem. Jesus was safe there from the Sanhedrin but close enough to walk to the Passover feast that was happening soon (John 11:55).

entries.title: John
entries.content: As crowds arrived in Jerusalem on pilgrimage for Passover (see John 2:13), the city was buzzing with talk about Jesus and his miracle of raising Lazarus from the dead. People wondered if Jesus would be obedient to the law and come to the city to celebrate or play it safe in the countryside. The priests and Pharisees knew that Jesus was faithful to the law and would attend the festival, so they tried to make the city a trap for him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilgrims from throughout Israel began arriving in Jerusalem the week before the Passover. The festival was on Thursday that year. Jesus arrived in the area late on the previous Friday, just before the Sabbath.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In this part of John’s Gospel, two stories move forward at the same time.

First, more and more people begin to praise Jesus. Their excitement reaches a high point when crowds welcome him into Jerusalem with shouts of joy (John 12:12–13).

Second, the religious authorities become more determined to arrest Jesus and put him to death. As public support grows, their opposition grows as well.

• John's Gospel describes three events that happened only days before Passover (John 12:1–11, John 12:12–19, John 12:20–36). Then he explains why most of the people refused to believe and describes the final public message spoken by Jesus (John 12:37–50).

entries.title: John
entries.content: those reclining: People usually sat or leaned back at a low table while eating.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Mary … anointed Jesus' feet. This was not awkward because Jews reclined at formal meals, but it was still a dramatic gesture (compare Matthew 26:6–16; Mark 14:3–9). 

• Nard was a valuable spice from North India. It was sweet, red, and smelled like the perfume made from the gladiola plant. Twelve ounces of nard cost one year's wages (John 12:5). 

According to Mark's Gospel, Mary also anointed the head of Jesus (Mark 14:3). The perfume ran down and made his clothes smell good (Mark 14:8).

• her hair: Women never took their hair covering off in public (see Luke 7:38). Mary was acting with deep and costly devotion.

entries.title: John
entries.content: three hundred denarii: Judas may have been exaggerating, but Mary’s sacrifice was certainly very costly.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Leave her alone: Jesus defended Mary by explaining her actions. The nard was a burial spice for his death. Jesus was readied for burial as he approached the hour of glorification and death (see study note on 12:23).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus would not ignore the poor. He cared deeply for people in need.

However, this moment to honor and serve him was unique. It was a special opportunity that would not happen again.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The next day was Sunday (see John 12:1). 

• A large crowd of religious travelers, many from Galilee, camped in this area. As Jesus traveled the road to Jerusalem, they cheered for him. This triumphal entry appears in all four Gospels (Matthew 21:1–11; Mark 11:1–11; Luke 19:29–38).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Palm branches: The date palm symbolized pride in the Jewish nation and celebration. 

• meet Him: The Greek word often describes crowds welcoming a king returning in triumph from a war. 

• Blessed is He: The crowd quoted Psalm 118:25–26, with a greeting for those who came to Jerusalem. 

The phrase "Blessed is the King of Israel!" is not in the psalm (but see Zephaniah 3:15). Although the people saw Jesus as a national political liberator, he rejected this role (John 6:15).

entries.title: John
entries.content: By choosing a young donkey instead of a warhorse, Jesus calmed the excited crowd that was eager for him to become king. He also fulfilled Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah (see Zechariah 9:9). He made it clear that his kingship was not based on violence. He did not come as a warrior to conquer nations. He came to give life. His rule would bring peace, not military victory.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The crowds did not fully understand who Jesus was. Even his disciples did not grasp the full meaning of what was happening. They saw the events, but they did not yet understand their true significance (their deeper meaning).

After Jesus was glorified (raised up in death, resurrection, and return to the Father), things changed. When the disciples received the Holy Spirit, they began to understand more clearly (see John 2:22).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This scene describes the highest point of the popularity of Jesus. At this time, large crowds followed him. Many people were excited about his teaching and his miracles.

entries.title: John
entries.content: the whole world (literally the world): The Pharisees' words were more meaningful than they realized. Jesus came to reach the world (John 3:17), and the Pharisees said that Jesus had accomplished his task.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Among those people attracted to Jesus were some Greeks who believed in Israel's God. They had come to the Passover feast to worship (John 12:19). The mission of Jesus was not only for Israel but for the entire world (John 10:16; John 11:52). After the resurrection of Jesus, the church's mission was to go beyond Judea to Samaria, and even to the ends of the earth (Matthew 28:19; Acts 1:8).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Greeks approached Philip because he had a Greek name and was most likely also Greek.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus often said that the hour had not yet come (John 2:4; John 7:30; John 8:20), but now it had. The arrival of the Greeks marked the beginning of the most important moment in the ministry of Jesus. This was the time of his glorification.

This happened when the saving work of Jesus on the cross was completed. He rose from the dead, gave the Holy Spirit, and returned to his place of glory in heaven (John 19:30; John 20:1–31; John 20:22; John 17:5, John 17:11). 

The connection with the Greeks who had come to Jerusalem was important (John 12:20). The public ministry of Jesus among the Jews was coming to an end. His mission was not limited to one nation. Through his death and resurrection, he would belong to the whole world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The central event of the glorification of Jesus was the cross (John 12:23). Like a kernel of wheat planted in the soil, the death of Jesus would bring abundant life.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
For disciples (followers of Jesus), sacrifice and self-effacement (choosing not to put oneself first) are part of this path. They do not lose life by following Jesus. Instead, they gain the fullness of life that comes through his sacrifice.

Those who renounce (turn away from) the world’s priorities will be with Jesus forever. God will honor those who serve his Son. In this way, the path of humble obedience leads to eternal life and honor.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
My soul is troubled: John used the same term (Greek tarassō) to describe the strong emotion of agony that Jesus felt when he stood before Lazarus’s tomb (John 11:33; also John 13:21). 

When Jesus faced his coming death, he was not without emotion. He did not act as if nothing troubled him. He experienced real anguish (deep sorrow and distress). Even in his distress, Jesus remained obedient to the Father’s will. Throughout his ministry, he had said that he did only what the Father sent him to do (John 5:19–23; John 6:37; John 8:29, John 8:38; John 14:31).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• A voice came from heaven: Compare Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5; Mark 1:11; Mark 9:7; Luke 3:22; Luke 9:35. 

• God had already brought glory to himself when Christ entered the world, and through the work of Jesus. This showed God's power to the world (John 1:14). 

• I will glorify it again: The final display of glory would come at the cross (see John 12:23; John 17:1). In John's Gospel, the cross is an event of glory as Christ was "lifted up" and glorified there (John 12:32). 

Jesus was prepared for crucifixion like a king coming to his coronation. The cross was like a throne (see John 19:19–22). They buried Jesus like a king. 

• The time of his glorification included all the events from his arrest through his resurrection.

entries.title: John
entries.content: It was impossible for people to comprehend what was happening with Jesus, and many of his signs led to confusion and division in the crowd. Only later did his disciples understand (John 2:22; John 12:16), when Jesus was glorified and the Spirit was given. Still, God’s voice symbolized his validation of his Son before the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• In John’s Gospel, judgment does not happen only on the final Judgment Day. It began when Jesus came into the world as the light (John 3:19; John 5:24; John 9:39). 

• Satan is the prince of this world. Satan promotes darkness, leads people into sin, and spreads death. Although Satan’s final defeat is still future, his power was broken through the work of Jesus (see Luke 10:17–18; Mark 3:27). 

Now Christ reigns as king in heaven (Acts 7:55–56; Ephesians 1:19–22).

entries.title: John
entries.content: when I am lifted up from the earth (see John 3:14; John 8:28): The crowd did not understand what Jesus meant. The Greek verb can also mean "be exalted" (Matthew 23:12). Or, it can refer to honor (Luke 10:15). In John's Gospel, the cross was not a place of shame for Jesus, but where his true glory was shown.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Many people in the time of Jesus believed that the Messiah would live forever and defeat his enemies. They expected a strong and victorious ruler.

Because of this belief, the words Jesus spoke confused them.

• Who is this Son of Man?: The Jews did not understand what sort of Messiah planned to die.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus was the Light (John 1:4, John 1:7–9; John 3:19–21; John 8:12). He urged the crowd to choose to believe in him before it was too late. 

• They could become sons of the light by being spiritually born through God's power (John 1:12–13). 

• was hidden from them: He first withdrew from Judea and then from this audience (John 11:54; John 12:36). Soon, he would withdraw from the world (John 17:11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus finished his work, but they still did not believe in him. His sermons before the world were complete and the signs had been displayed, but he was rejected (John 1:11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: they were unable to believe: John quotes Isaiah 6:10 to explain Israel's lack of belief (see Matthew 13:13–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; Acts 28:26–27). When God's revelation comes, we must believe. If we refuse, the light disappears (John 12:35–36). When God’s light departs, the darkness closes over unbelieving hearts. This means that continued rejection leads to deeper spiritual blindness.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The prophet Isaiah had seen the glory of the Messiah and how the world would respond (see Isaiah 6:10).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Many people did believe in Jesus. However, they were afraid to admit it in public.

They feared the reaction of the religious leaders and the social consequences that might follow.

To follow Jesus means more than private belief. It includes openly identifying with him and telling others about him, even when this may bring rejection (John 1:35–51; John 4:1–42).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus makes a final appeal for faith in him. These verses summarize chapters John 1:1–12. The Father sent Jesus, who is the only source of his ministry. Jesus is the light shining in darkness to bring salvation and eternal life to all who believe in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The greatest error is for people to see the light and reject it, thinking it has no connection with the Father who sent the light.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The setting is the final Passover meal of Jesus on Thursday evening. During this meal, Judas Iscariot betrays Jesus. John does not describe the meal itself like the Synoptic Gospels do (Matthew 26:17–29; Mark 14:12–25; Luke 22:7–20; see also 1 Corinthians 11:23–26). John focuses on other activities at the event, such as:

• the foot washing (John 13:1–17), 

• Judas’s betrayal (John 13:18–30), and 

• the prediction of Peter’s denials (John 13:31–38).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This section focuses on the sign of the cross, the great climax of the life of Jesus, as well as the time Jesus spent preparing his disciples for it (chapters John 13:13–17). Each event during these important days glorified Jesus. His arrest, trial, death on the cross, and resurrection all bring forth responses of awe. On the cross, Jesus is "lifted up" in glory before the world (John 12:32).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Judas … Iscariot: He had refused to trust in Jesus. Darkness consumed him and he became a tool of the devil (compare study note on 12:39–40).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Foot washing was common in Greek and Jewish cultures as a daily routine. It was also a common gesture when hosting guests (see Luke 7:36–50). It was a humble task designated for servants. When Jesus began to wash the disciples’ feet, he assumed the role of a servant.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Knowing how committed Peter was to Jesus, it makes sense that he protested. However, Jesus was not just showing Peter how to serve. This was a symbolic introduction of the greater sacrifice Jesus would make on the cross (John 13:7). Receiving spiritual cleansing from Jesus is necessary for discipleship. If Peter could not accept this act, he could not be a disciple of Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content: my hands and my head as well: Peter misunderstood Jesus (compare John 2:19–20; John 3:3–4). Peter thought having more water meant having more of Jesus. Everything became obvious to Peter only when he received the Holy Spirit (for example, see Acts 2:14–36).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus was pointing to a deeper cleansing through his sacrifice.

He was not speaking only about washing the body. He was speaking about being made clean in a complete way.

Through his death, he makes a person clean all over. This means forgiveness of sin and a restored relationship with God.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus performed acts of humble service, such as washing his disciples’ feet and giving his life on the cross. By doing this, he set an example for others to follow. He showed that true greatness is expressed through love, service, and personal sacrifice for others.

• wash one another's feet: Foot washing was a common act in that culture. Because of this, some think that Jesus meant for his followers to repeat this action in a literal way. Others believe he used it as a symbol of humble service.

In either case, the main point is clear. Jesus wants his followers to serve others with humility and self-giving love. Servanthood and sacrifice should mark their lives.

entries.title: John
entries.content: no servant is greater than his master: This saying was popular and appears in a number of passages (see also John 15:20; Matthew 10:24; Luke 6:40). Here, Jesus meant that the servant should follow the master's example of sacrifice.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• I am not speaking about all of you: This is the third time Jesus mentions that Judas will betray him (John 13:2, John 13:11). This matter deeply "troubled" Jesus (John 13:21). 

• I know whom I have chosen: This does not mean Jesus only chose the 11 disciples and excluded Judas. Jesus chose Judas and gave him every opportunity to believe. He realized that Judas had chosen the darkness instead of the light (John 6:70).

• The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me: Eating together was a cultural symbol of personal intimacy, which made Judas’s betrayal all the more serious.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Judas’s betrayal did not surprise Jesus. It should also not surprise his disciples when it happens. 

• that I am He: By using the phrase I am, Jesus clearly identified himself with the God of the Old Testament. See Exodus 3:14.

entries.title: John
entries.content: For the third time in the Gospel of John, Jesus became troubled (Greek tarassō; see John 11:33; John 12:27). When Judas betrayed Jesus, it caused him deep grief.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The disciple whom Jesus loved is appears:

• at the cross (John 19:26–27),

• at the tomb (John 20:2–9), and

• and at the resurrection (John 21:1, John 21:20–23). 

He also wrote the Gospel of John (John 21:24–25). Some scholars believe that Lazarus was in fact the disciple whom Jesus loved (see John 11:3, John 11:5, John 11:36). The person referred to here was among the 12 apostles, so most people identify the disciple whom Jesus loved as the apostle John. 

• was reclining at His side: They were likely reclining at a triclinium, a U-shaped table with couches around it. Guests reclined on the couches, while the center allowed those serving to access them. Those who were eating supported themselves with their left elbows and used their right hands to eat. They extended their feet away from the table (compare Luke 7:38).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Peter told the disciple sitting next to Jesus ("the one whom Jesus loved") to ask who would betray him (John 13:23). As the disciple was reclining next to Jesus, he leaned over and spoke to Jesus in private.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Meals included flat bread, which those eating would dip into a shared bowl. Jesus gave a piece to Judas (compare Ruth 2:14). The disciples might have thought Jesus was honoring him. 

They did not understand what was happening. They even thought that when Judas left, it was to fulfill an official duty for the feast (John 13:29). However, Jesus was signaling to Judas that he knew Judas's plan and was not surprised. The knowledge Jesus has is deep and complete (see John 1:48; John 2:25).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Satan entered into him: Judas became an example of what happens to people consumed by the darkness (see Luke 22:3). Satan uses such people as tools in a wider struggle against the light.

• What you are about to do, do quickly: By giving this command, Jesus again showed he was in control, not human beings or Satan (see study note on John 7:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content: None of the others suspected that something odd was happening. Passover evening was one of the only nights when the city gates were left open. The night was spent in prayer and meditation, money was given to the poor, and provisions were always needed for this complex meal.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
out into the night: This detail is more than a note about the time of day. It has symbolic meaning.

Judas’s departure shows his spiritual condition. Darkness had taken hold of him completely (see study note on 13:2; compare John 3:19). Jesus, the light of the world, is the opposite of the night.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The time had come. Judas’s departure into the night marked a clear turning point in the story of the Gospel. Jesus was now left with his closest friends, as the hour of his glory was beginning. This period began with Judas’s betrayal and ended with the resurrection.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Old Testament and later Jewish literature include numerous examples of farewells in which a dying person offers last words to intimate friends (see Gen 49:1–27; Deut 31–34; Josh 23–24; 1 Samuel 12:1 Sam 12; 1 Chr 28:1–29:30). Such farewells used a standard form. The dying person, surrounded by his loved ones, comforted them and exhorted them to obey the law. He prayed and blessed them and often left behind some writings. In some cases, the departing person passed on his “spirit” to his followers or his successor (see Num 27:18; Deut 34:9; 2 Kgs 2:9–14). Each of these elements is present in Jesus’ farewell. • This section is often called the Upper Room Discourse, since the meal was taken in an “upstairs room” (Luke 22:12).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus addressed the apostles as his children, marking the start of his farewell address.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The command for the disciples to love one another was not new (see Leviticus 19:18). However, loving each other as Jesus loved was a dramatic change. Jesus showed his love for God through perfect obedience (John 14:31). Now, he commanded that disciples show their love for him through committed obedience.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Peter claimed to be ready to die for Jesus. But Peter is well known for denying Jesus (John 18:15–18, John 18:25–27; see also Matthew 26:32–34; Mark 14:27–30; Luke 22:31–34). Although Peter's courage and loyalty failed, Jesus forgave and restored him (John 21:15–19).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus felt troubled (Greek tarassō) on three occasions (John 11:33; John 12:27; John 13:21). His trust in God's power helped him confront these difficult times. When the disciples heard the upsetting words of John 13:33, they felt the same way. 

• believe (or trust, or have faith) in God: Only trusting God would help them through his hour of death.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus provided answers to his disciples’ many spoken and unspoken concerns.

entries.title: John
entries.content: In My Father’s house are many rooms: God's house is where he lives (Revelation 21:9–22:5). The Greek word for rooms comes from a verb meaning "remain, abide, dwell." Jesus promises his followers a place to live with him, wherever he is. Later, this house becomes a spiritual presence. Jesus makes his home in the hearts of his followers through the Holy Spirit (John 14:23). This means that believers carry God’s presence inside them.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Some scholars think that Jesus meant he would come and get his followers after the resurrection (John 14:18). Others think these words refer to the second coming of Jesus. For the disciples, the return of Jesus from the grave was more important (chapter John 16:16).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• I am: See study note on 6:35. You can only access the Father through Jesus, who is the way and the truth and the life. 

• The way to the Father is only through Jesus. Other religions and philosophies suggest different ways to God. But Jesus claimed he is the only way to God. 

• Jesus is the truth because God is truth. 

• God is the source of eternal life. At Lazarus’s tomb, Jesus demonstrated his divine power over life and death (John 11:25).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Philip did not yet understand that in Jesus he was seeing the full embodiment of God (John 14:9).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father: Compare John 1:1–2. Jesus Christ is God in human body (John 1:14). This explains his ability to perform divine works. Jesus did not just teach about God, he is God. Jesus's remarkable statement here echoed what he said at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah): “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). This claim is the reason for the world's opposition to Christ (John 5:18).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus made surprising and powerful claims about himself (John 10:30, John 10:37–38). However, true faith recognizes the close union between Jesus and God the Father. To believe in Jesus is to trust that he truly reveals and represents the Father.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus promised that those who believe in him would do great works and pray with confidence (see 1 John 5:14). This would happen after Jesus returned to the Father, when he sent the Holy Spirit to give them strength and guidance (John 14:16). 

• The greater things will not surpass what Jesus did. Instead, ordinary people will do these works because the Holy Spirit gives them power. God promised that in the era of the Spirit, he would bring his kingdom and power into the world in a new way.

entries.title: John
entries.content: If you love me: Because Jesus loves the Father, he is obedient to what God directs him to say and do (John 12:49). If we love him, we will obey him, too (John 14:21, John 14:23; John 15:10, John 15:14; see 1 John 2:3–4; 1 John 5:2).

entries.title: John
entries.content: another Advocate: The Spirit continues the work of Jesus by advising, defending, and protecting believers.

entries.title: John
entries.content: the Spirit of truth: The Holy Spirit communicates the truth about God (see also John 15:26; John 16:13). The Spirit maintains the presence of Jesus in the world, continuing and supporting the work Jesus began.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus had already assured his followers that they would not be spiritual orphans and that he would return to them (John 14:1–4). While he is away, they will be filled with the Spirit, who will sustain them with his presence (John 14:12–17).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The resurrection of Jesus began a new spiritual union with his disciples (John 14:19). This union is like the close relationship he has with the Father (see John 15:4–5; 1 John 1:3).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Several men named Judas appear in the New Testament. Judas, the brother of Jesus, wrote the letter of Jude (Mark 6:3). Luke 6:16 lists Judas, the son of James, as a disciple (John mentions this Judas in this verse). He is also known as Thaddaeus (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18). 

• Lord, why: Judas asked an important question. If Jesus planned to return powerfully from death, why not use the chance to show himself plainly to the world? Why not prove his power and identity?

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus answered Judas's question. He said his coming would be a deep spiritual revelation that the world would not understand. 

• The coming of Jesus would happen in three events: 

• his resurrection, 

• the arrival of the Holy Spirit, and 

• his second coming. 

When he comes through the Spirit, he and the Father will live within Christians, making a home with each of them (see study note on 14:2).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit (see also John 14:16; John 15:26; John 16:7, John 16:12–14). 

• The Holy Spirit … will teach you all things: The Holy Spirit will teach the disciples everything. He will help them remember the words of Jesus and understand what those words mean. John experienced this help from the Spirit as he wrote his gospel (John 2:22). Christians also experience this work of the Spirit as they hear and study the Scriptures.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Jewish greeting peace (Hebrew shalom) shows the goal of the work of Jesus on earth: to restore humanity's relationship with God (Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 57:19; Romans 5:1). The resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit helped complete this work (John 14:28).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Father is greater than I am: See also John 5:19–20. Jesus is submissive to the Father but is also one with the Father (John 10:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content: the prince of this world: Satan did not control the events in Jerusalem that led to the cross. The death of Jesus on the cross was not an accident, and Jesus was not a helpless victim. Instead, Jesus obeyed God's plan.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I am: See study note on 6:35. The vine and the vineyard have traditionally represented God’s people. He "plants and tends" them in Israel (Psalm 80:8–18; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Jeremiah 12:10–11; Ezekiel 15:1–5; Hosea 10:1–2). When Jesus used this image, he made an important change. He declared that he is the true vine and that a relationship with God requires attachment to him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus prepared his disciples for his departure, instructing them to remain in close fellowship with him. The image of a grapevine illustrates both intimacy and fruitfulness. To sustain genuine spiritual life in the world, believers must remain intimately connected to Christ.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Gardeners cut away dead branches and trim healthy branches so they will produce more fruit. Fruitfulness is the result of life-giving connection to the vine.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The term remain (Greek menō) is important for understanding John 15:4–10. A growing disciple, in whom the Father and the Son live through the Spirit, must be continuously connected to Christ (see John 14:16–25; John 15:26).

entries.title: John
entries.content: \Anyone who does not remain in Christ is separated from the vine and its life. A living branch produces clusters of grapes (John 15:5). Connection with the vine allows the life of Jesus to flow fruitfully through the disciple. Those who claim to be attached to Christ but yield no fruit are useless and will be burned.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Those whose lives are in harmony with Jesus may ask for anything because their prayers are controlled by his word. Their prayers will be answered and bring glory to God (John 14:10–13).

entries.title: John
entries.content: True disciples will experience a transformed, fruit-bearing life because they live in a relationship of love with both Jesus and the Father (John 15:9–10).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Just as Jesus demonstrated his love for the Father by obeying his will (John 14:31), the disciples of Jesus show their love by obeying him (John 13:34–35; John 14:15; 1 John 2:5; 1 John 5:2–3).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• This is My commandment … love each other: See John 13:34. 

• Jesus demonstrated his love by sacrificing his life at the cross.

entries.title: John
entries.content: God considered Abraham and Moses to be his friends (Exodus 33:11; 2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23). This is the closest relationship possible between God and a person. Jesus chooses his friends (John 15:16). They demonstrate their friendship by obeying him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The disciples of a rabbi were considered his servants or slaves. Jesus elevated his followers to a higher relationship as his friends.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Disciples must be like their master in every way. They must show love and obedience and experience opposition from those against their message (John 15:20–21; see John 9:1–41; John 11:16). Darkness opposes light (John 1:5). The followers of Jesus carry that light in the world (1 John 1:7; 1 John 2:9). They should expect the world to hate them in the way it hated Jesus (see John 17:14). The disciples of Jesus share his separation from and conflict with the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: No servant is greater than his master: See study note on 13:16. The disciples of Jesus should live like him in every way, even when they face suffering or death because of their faith.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Now, however, they have no excuse: The ministry of Jesus provided both words and works as evidence that pointed to God (John 15:22; John 15:24). Once people have heard and seen him, they are accountable.

entries.title: John
entries.content: They hated Me without reason: This Old Testament citation shows the unjustified anger of people who live in the darkness, meaning those who oppose God’s truth.

entries.title: John
entries.content: When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth: Like a legal representative, the Holy Spirit is counselor and protector of the followers of Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Disciples are not alone when they testify about Christ (Matthew 28:20). The Holy Spirit is with them and gives them the words to say (Matthew 10:19–20).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus had described the coming conflicts so the disciples would not abandon their faith (literally be caused to stumble (John 15:18–25). The biggest challenge they would encounter was rejecting their faith in front of their opponents (see Matthew 23:34; Luke 6:22). This would especially be true during the difficult times ahead (see John 12:35; 1 John 2:9–11).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
the Advocate: This title refers to the Holy Spirit. The word can mean helper, comforter, or one who speaks on behalf of another.

Jesus taught that the Spirit would come after his departure and glorification (his death, resurrection, and return to the Father; see John 7:37–39; John 14:16, John 14:26; John 15:26; John 16:12–14).

The Spirit was a promised gift. After Jesus returned to the Father, the Spirit would guide, teach, and strengthen his followers.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
The Holy Spirit unveils to the world:

• the real nature of its sin, 

• the truth about righteousness found only in God, and 

• the coming judgment.

In one sense, this judgment has already begun. When God’s light shines into the darkness, it exposes what is wrong and calls people to respond.

entries.title: John
entries.content: One of the Spirit’s roles is to convict the world. Convict is a legal term: The world had conducted its trial of Jesus, examining the evidence for his case (his signs and claims). Now the world would stand trial before the Spirit, and its guilt would be proven.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The judgment of sinners had already started. This was because God had already judged the prince of this world, Satan (see John 12:31). The world believed it was judging Jesus, but the opposite was true.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The Spirit of truth, who brings truth from God, guides the judgment of the world. 

• The Spirit speaks only what he hears from the Father. The Father, Son, and Spirit work in perfect unity (John 16:15). The disciples could expect the Spirit to reveal new things about the present and future (see John 14:26).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus reassured the disciples that his departure (on the cross) would be short and his return (in the resurrection) would be soon. When they saw him again, the disciples would experience overwhelming joy and intimacy with him in the Spirit.

entries.title: John
entries.content: a little while: Jesus repeated this phrase to comfort his disciples. He wanted them to know that their separation from him would not last long. Although he would soon leave them, he would return to them again.

entries.title: John
entries.content: With the death of Jesus on the cross, the world thought it had won a victory over the light. The surprise of the cross would cause the disciples to weep and mourn, but their sorrow would change to joy when Jesus defeated the grave (John 20:20).

entries.title: John
entries.content: pain in childbirth: This metaphor symbolizes anguish that is followed by God's blessing and wonder (compare Isaiah 21:2–3; Isaiah 26:16–21; Isaiah 66:7–10; Jeremiah 13:21).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Ask and you will receive: Two notable effects of the resurrection are the joy of understanding and the joy of successful prayer. The disciples would no longer experience the confusion described in John 16:16–18.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus spoke using figures of speech, which could only be interpreted with God’s help (1 Corinthians 1:18–25). With the coming of the Holy Spirit, the disciples would understand.

entries.title: John
entries.content: After the resurrection of Jesus, the Holy Spirit brought a close relationship with God. Through the Spirit, disciples could live in God’s presence and speak to the Father about their needs (John 14:23).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
take courage; I have overcome the world!: “Such a saying as this is worthy to be carried from Rome to Jerusalem on one’s knees” (Martin Luther). The final words of Jesus did not rebuke his disciples. Instead, he spoke to comfort them. Jesus promised peace and joy (John 14:27; John 16:20, John 16:22). 

Now he added that his disciples can discover peace even when surrounded by threats. They can remain calm even when others oppose their faith.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus looked up to heaven. This was the traditional Jewish way to pray (John 11:41; Psalm 123:1). He probably also raised his hands (Exodus 9:33; Exodus 17:11; Psalm 28:2). Jesus said prayers like this out loud so his followers could hear them (John 11:41–42; John 12:27–30; also Matthew 11:25–30; Luke 10:21–22). 

• Father was the usual way Jesus addressed God, which he did six times in this prayer (see also John 11:41; John 12:27). This title, uncommon in the Jewish faith, showed the intimate relationship Jesus has with God. 

• the hour: This hour included the betrayal of Jesus by Judas, his arrest, torture, death, and resurrection (see study note on 12:23).

• Glorify your Son: In the Gospel of John, the cross is a place of honor. The unity of Jesus with the Father means that if the Son receives glory, the Father will also receive glory.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
This chapter contains the longest prayer of Jesus. People often refer to it as the "high priestly prayer." The prayer shows the deepest concerns and purposes of Jesus. 

This prayer concludes his last words that began at John 13:31. Jesus expressed his own concerns to his Father (John 17:1–8). He then expressed concerns for the church and its future (John 17:9–26).

entries.title: John
entries.content: All authority has been placed in Jesus’ hands (John 3:35); he can give eternal life as only God can (John 3:15; John 5:21, John 5:25–26).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• that they may know you: In the Hebrew language, "knowing" includes experience and intimacy. For Christians, this means loving God and obeying him. 

• whom You have sent: Jesus came from heaven and was returning (John 17:5). So he has divine authority as God's agent.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The miracles of Jesus displayed God's glory to the world (John 1:14). This task was finished. The life and obedience of Jesus glorified God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus prayed to return to the position he had with God before the world began (John 1:1).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This verse summarizes what Jesus came to do. He revealed the true person of God to the world, gathered up God’s people into his flock, and instructed them in obedience. The result of this work is the church.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus revealed himself to the world. Those who received his message became children of God (John 1:12; John 11:52). He revealed God's word to them.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus prayed for his disciples, who must continue his work after his departure.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Just as the Son brings glory to the Father (John 17:1, John 17:4–5), the disciples bring the Son glory (John 17:22). The love and obedience that brought glory to God in the life of Jesus become features of his disciples’ lives.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The first concern Jesus had for his disciples was that they would remain united with each other in the same way he is one with the Father.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Until now, Jesus had guarded his followers. Now he was concerned for their strength and survival in his absence, because the world would be hostile toward them and their mission of challenging the world by preaching the truth (John 15:18–27; John 16:8–11). After Jesus departed to heaven, the Holy Spirit would protect them and bring them joy (John 15:26).

entries.title: John
entries.content: God’s word, which Jesus had given his disciples, also provides a defense against the world. The Spirit would preserve and recall God’s word in the church (John 14:26), equipping the church for its encounter with the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Sanctify: This refers to purity gained by separation from the world, and living a life so aligned with God that it reflects Disciples are set apart by God, equipped by the Spirit, and prepared by God’s word to enter the world without being victimized by its darkness.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I sanctify Myself: Priests and prophets were similarly set apart for service to God (Leviticus 8:30; Jeremiah 1:5). Jesus again committed himself to God's mission. He recognized that he was set apart for the purpose of the cross. The disciples would benefit because his death would enable them to experience new holiness in a deep attachment to God.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus was praying for other sheep who were not yet in his flock (John 10:16). These are the believers through the centuries who have come to faith through the witness of the disciples of Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Be one: For believers, becoming one with one another is an outgrowth of the union they enjoy with Jesus himself, a union modeled on the oneness of the Father and the Son. 

• May they also be in Us: Through the Holy Spirit's power, believers experience a profound and intimate union with the Father and the Son, leading to transformation (John 14:20, John 14:23; 1 John 4:13).

• Disciples of Jesus represent him, so their right actions and relationships with each other reflect the credibility of Christ in the world. When there is disunity, infighting, and intolerance, their testimony to the world is unconvincing. When people observe the community of believers, they know that it represents Jesus; a unified, loving community convinces the world to believe (John 13:35; 1 John 3:11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The community of believers should display the same glory that Jesus displayed from the Father.

entries.title: John
entries.content: so that the world may know: If the church lives in the Spirit, reflects God’s glory and love, and shows unity sustained by a shared knowledge of God, then its testimony will amaze the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I want those You have given Me to be with Me: Someday, all the followers of Jesus will see his true glory and the love that has existed in heaven before the beginning of time (John 17:5). Jesus was returning to heaven and deeply wanted to see his disciples there so that they might witness what words on earth cannot describe.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• All who accept the Son and embrace the Father will experience the kind of love known only between the Father and the Son. 

• I in them: Jesus loves his followers and wants to fill them with glory and joy that compares to nothing in the world.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley. This was a dry river valley (a wadi) outside the eastern walls of Jerusalem. 

• a garden: This is the Garden of Gethsemane (Mark 14:32). This garden was a group of olive trees on the west side of the Mount of Olives. The Aramaic name gath shemaney means “olive press.” Jesus liked this place and often prayed there (see John 8:1; Luke 21:37; Luke 22:39).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus finished speaking his final words to his disciples in the upper room (John 13:31–17:26). Jesus then left the city and went to a garden east of Jerusalem to pray. There, authorities arrested him and took him back into the city for questioning by the Jewish religious leaders. The important "hour" Jesus often mentioned throughout the Gospel had arrived (see John 2:4; see also study note on 12:23).

entries.title: John
entries.content: John’s full account of the group that arrested him adds details not mentioned in the other Gospels. The temple authorities sent Roman soldiers and temple guards. While the temple guards arrested Jesus, the Roman soldiers stood by to prevent a riot. The Roman group was large enough to need a commander. They came with weapons and were expecting a struggle (John 18:10, 12). Many people claimed to be the Messiah. Often, they tried to force the Romans out of the land, which caused political conflict.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I am He (literally I am): Jesus identified himself by the divine name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see Exodus 3:14; see also John 4:26; John 8:24, John 8:58).

entries.title: John
entries.content: All the soldiers and guards fell back before the Lord (compare Isaiah 6:5; Ezekiel 1:28; Daniel 10:9; Acts 9:4; Revelation 1:17). Even the Roman soldiers, who were trained to stand firm, fell to the ground before Christ. They did this to show submission, but they did not fully understand what had happened and went on with the arrest.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I am He: Jesus used God's divine name for the second time (see study note on 18:5).

entries.title: John
entries.content: I have not lost one: Jesus continued to be a good shepherd, offering his life for the sheep and protecting them from the wolves (John 10:11–15). From the beginning, however, Judas Iscariot had not been a true disciple of Jesus (John 17:12).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Simon Peter drew his sword: This was a short sword or long knife, usually worn with everyday clothes.

• The Hebrew name Malchus means "king." John may have included this detail as a subtle wordplay pointing to the true identity of Jesus (see John 18:36–37; John 19:19).

• Put your sword back: The mission of Jesus was not to fight for his life, but to die for ours.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Soldiers bound Jesus and took him back to Jerusalem. 

• First, they brought him to Annas, who had been the high priest and remained very influential. Five of his sons also became high priests. Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was the official high priest at that time (see John 18:24).

entries.title: John
entries.content: one man died for the people: Caiaphas had said this as a political calculation (John 11:49–50). John points out the irony: the death of Jesus did not bring political freedom to Israel. Instead, it brought spiritual salvation for everyone who believes in him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: another disciple: The other disciple is not named but was probably "the one whom Jesus loved" (John 13:23). This disciple was the apostle John and the author of this book.

entries.title: John
entries.content: While Annas was questioning Jesus, the girl watching the door asked Peter if he was one of the disciples of Jesus (John 18:12–14, John 18:19–24). Jesus confronted his questioners and denied nothing. But Peter quickly denied his connection to Jesus three times (John 18:17, John 18:25, John 18:27).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The high priest asked Jesus questions, which went against Jewish legal procedures. In Jewish court, the priest did not directly question the person on the defense. Instead, they gathered evidence from witnesses to prove guilt (see Numbers 35:30; Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15; compare Matthew 18:16). If Jesus said anything that would make him guilty, Annas would use it against him at his trial. Annas tried to follow Roman practice by making Jesus say something about himself that would make him guilty. This was different than using witnesses as Jewish law required.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus's direct response reminded Annas that everything was public knowledge. This exposed the priest's attempt to follow Roman practice.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
When Jesus reminded Annas about the correct legal procedure, one of the temple guards thought he was being disrespectful. The guard slapped Jesus.

However, Jesus knew the law well and spoke truthfully. There were no witnesses accusing him, and no evidence was presented against him.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Annas could say no more. His questioning had failed. So he sent Jesus to Caiaphas to be tried before the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's judicial high council (see Mark 14:53–15:1).

entries.title: John
entries.content: He denied it: Peter denied knowing Jesus three times. Later, Jesus asked Peter three times to reaffirm his love (John 21:15–17).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The trial before Caiaphas ended in the early hours of the morning. The Sanhedrin (Jewish high council) did not have the power to execute someone. They needed Pilate, the Roman governor, to carry out an execution (John 18:31). 

• They did not want to become ritually unclean by contact with Gentiles in Pilate’s headquarters. So Pilate, probably fearing a riot, went outside to meet them. 

• The Passover meal itself had taken place the night before (see John 13:1; Mark 14:14–16). The next day, another meal began the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread (Leviticus 23:5–6).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilate, the fifth Roman governor of Judea, ruled the country from AD 26 to 36. He usually lived on the coast in Caesarea, but kept troops stationed in a fortress in Jerusalem where he appeared personally for major festivals. He was a brutal ruler whose atrocities against the Jews were legendary (for example, Luke 13:1; Josephus, War 2.9.2–4).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Pilate did not consider the charges convincing. So he told the Sanhedrin to judge Jesus by their own law. Pilate saw this as a Jewish argument, which he refused to investigate. 

However, the Jewish leaders insisted that execution was necessary. This fulfilled the prediction Jesus made about how he would die (see John 12:32–33). The Jews would have used stoning, but the Romans used crucifixion. If Pilate sentenced Jesus, the Romans would hang Jesus on a cross to die.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Pilate was personally responsible for capital crimes in which the interests and security of the Roman Empire were at stake, so he began his formal legal inquiry.

• Are You the King of the Jews?: To get the governor’s attention, Caiaphas accused Jesus of telling people not to pay taxes to Rome and claiming to be a king (Luke 23:2). To Pilate, Jesus might have seemed like another Jewish terrorist or revolutionary with ideas about the Messiah and a group of armed followers (see Luke 23:18–19; Acts 5:36–37).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The response Jesus gave forced the governor to reveal the origin of his question. The temple leaders were responsible for these accusations. Pilate only wanted to know if Jesus was a rebel who might threaten Roman interests.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus was willing to accept the title of king, but he made it clear that he did not govern an earthly kingdom that might rival Rome. The kingship of Jesus is not of this world. Rather than being a political ruler, he rules through the devotion and obedience of his followers.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• What is truth?: Truth was not a foreign idea to Pilate. But he did not wait for an answer because he did not believe there was one. 

• Pilate returned to the council members waiting outside and delivered his verdict: not guilty. Although he referred to Jesus as “King of the Jews” (see also John 19:19), the title was just an expression meant to mock Jesus. Pilate wanted to release Jesus. His offer showed that he did not want Jesus to be executed.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus was not a threat to Rome, but Barabbas was a revolutionary. He was a violent man involved in political uprisings. Barabbas had proven his capacity to challenge the Roman military occupation of Israel (see Luke 23:19).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilate had Jesus beaten after his sentencing (Mark 15:15). However, John here describes an earlier beating. This was likely Pilate's attempt to show that Jesus had been punished and he could release him (John 19:4). When this failed, Pilate passed his sentence and handed Jesus over to the Jewish leaders for crucifixion (John 19:16).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The crown of thorns might have come from a date palm tree (compare John 12:13–14). There are Greek coin images showing such crowns, with the stems woven and the thorns radiating upward above the crown. 

• The purple robe was probably a soldier's robe. It was dark red, completing the picture of mock royalty.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Pilate wanted to show Jesus to the crowd, hoping they would see his injuries and agree to release him. After being beaten with a whip with lead tips, Jesus was bleeding heavily.

• Pilate again declared that Jesus was not guilty, but the crowd loudly demanded his death (John 19:6).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilate knew that a riot could happen when a man popular with the masses was executed, so he shifted responsibility to crucify Jesus to the temple leaders.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• During the trial before Caiaphas, the charge of blasphemy (calling himself the Son of God) was determined to be the true crime Jesus had committed (see Mark 14:61–65). 

• The leaders had already tried to set Jesus against Roman interests and they would do it again (John 18:33; John 19:12). Now they challenged the governor in different way. Pilate had to maintain peace by enforcing local law, even if it did not matter to Rome. Claiming to be God's son was not illegal. Even Israel's kings did this (Psalms 2:7; Psalms 89:22–27). However, Jesus claimed to have God's divine authority, which they considered blasphemy (see John 5:18).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Pilate … was even more afraid: Pilate was superstitious, and stories of gods appearing in the world were not uncommon (Acts 14:11). He sensed more than a political fight was happening, so he asked Jesus, "Where are you from?" Pilate was not asking where Jesus was born. He was asking if Jesus was a divine man who came down from heaven. 

• Why Jesus did not answer is uncertain. Perhaps Pilate would not have understood that true power comes only from God, who had empowered Jesus (compare John 19:11).

entries.title: John
entries.content: You would have no authority over Me: Pilate had the power to crucify Jesus, but only because God gave him this temporary power. He allowed Pilate to have this power so that Jesus could advance toward the cross (see John 10:18).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Pilate tried to release Jesus each time they talked. Despite his efforts, he failed. 

• friend of Caesar: This was an official title for those, like senators, who showed great loyalty to the Roman emperor. The Jewish religious leaders implied they would damage Pilate's career by claiming he did not support Rome's interests. They probably knew that Pilate was also having a personal crisis.

Pilate’s patron in Rome, Sejanus, was the chief administrator of the empire under Tiberius Caesar. Sejanus had fallen from favor and was executed in AD 31. Pilate had every reason to be afraid.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Pilate sat on the governor’s judgment seat to give his verdict. In Greek, the word for this seat is bēma (compare Acts 25:6, “seat in court”).

• The Stone Pavement was the platform for the judgment seat. From there, Pilate spoke with the authority of his office.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The day of Preparation for the Passover: Here, Passover refers to the entire Feast of Unleavened Bread, not just the Jewish Passover meal from the night before. It was Friday, the preparation day for the Passover Sabbath. The Sabbath would start when the sun set (compare Mark 15:42; Luke 23:54).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The final words of the priests, “We have no king but Caesar,” are a contradiction of the Old Testament belief that God was Israel’s king (compare Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7; 1 Samuel 10:19). Jerusalem and its religious leaders were killing their true king while honoring Caesar, the pagan king of Rome (John 18:37).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilate handed Jesus over to the Roman soldiers. They prepared him for crucifixion with a second flogging, which nearly killed him (Mark 15:15). Jesus bled heavily, and his clothes were soaked in blood. The crown of thorns pressed deeply into his head. Nearly in shock, the soldiers forced Jesus to march to a site outside the city.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The vertical beam (Latin staticulum) of the cross usually stayed at the crucifixion site. The victim carried only the heavy cross beam (Latin patibulum). 

• Crucifixions were public executions near major roads. The Romans designed them to shock and warn the people. 

• The Place of the Skull (Hebrew and Aramaic Golgotha; Latin calvariae, “Calvary”): Most archaeologists agree that the crucifixion of Jesus happened at the site of the modern Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This is in the Christian Quarter of the old walled city of Jerusalem. 

An alternative site, Gordon’s Calvary (north of the Damascus Gate), shows what the scene might have looked like. However, it only has a tomb from the 500s BC, so it is unlikely to be where Jesus was crucified and buried.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
None of the writers of the Gospels focus on the details of being nailed to the cross because people already knew it was horrible. The soldiers used the cross as a tool for torture. They wanted victims to live for a while, sometimes for days. 

Because the Sabbath would begin when the sun set, they sped up the crucifixion of Jesus (John 19:31). Jesus had been severely beaten with whips tipped with stone or metal, so his back was deeply cut, and he was bleeding heavily.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Pilate posted a sign on the cross. Roman soldiers usually provided a written notice of the criminal’s name and crimes. As a possible act of revenge against the Jewish high council, Pilate ordered the sign to identify Jesus of Nazareth as the King of the Jews. The sign was posted in three languages for the whole world to understand.

entries.title: John
entries.content: As was their common practice, the Roman soldiers divided his clothes. The soldiers gambled for his valuable robe, which was seamless, rather than dividing it up.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• This is the only reference to the sister of the mother of Jesus in the New Testament. She might have been the wife of Zebedee and the mother of James and John (compare Matthew 27:56). This would make Jesus and John cousins. If so, it would help explain why Jesus asked the disciple he loved (John) to care for Mary (John’s aunt). 

• This is the only place that mentions Mary, the wife of Clopas. She might be the same as Mary, the mother of James and Joseph (compare Matthew 27:56). 

• Jesus healed Mary Magdalene, a woman from the village of Magdala (Mark 16:9; Luke 8:2). 

• Woman was a respectful and polite way of speaking in that culture (see John 2:4).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Here is your mother: Jesus used a Jewish family law to assign one person's care to another. This scene had additional importance: The people present represented the new community of the church that was born at the cross. Jesus wanted them to care for each other, following his command to love one another (John 13:34; John 15:12, John 15:17).

entries.title: John
entries.content: In Egypt, people used the hyssop bush to apply lamb's blood on door posts and its upper threshold (lintel) during the first Passover (Exodus 12:22). Jesus is God's Passover lamb, and his blood also saves (John 1:29, John 1:36).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus called out in triumph and exhaustion that he had finished the work he set out to do. On the cross he was not a victim, but a servant doing God’s bidding.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The Jewish authorities, eager to complete the crucifixion before Sabbath began at dusk, asked Pilate to break the legs of the men. It was common to break the legs of those crucified with a tool. It caused them to stop breathing and bleed excessively because the victim could not push themselves up to breathe.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• To confirm that Jesus was dead, a Roman soldier stabbed his side with a spear. 

• blood and water flowed out: This has several levels of meaning: 

• The spear probably cut through the pericardium, the sack around the heart, releasing these fluids. 

• John might have been thinking of more Passover symbolism. The Passover lamb’s blood had to flow as it died. 

• The water flowing from the side of Jesus is similar to the language of "living water" that Jesus had mentioned earlier (see John 4:10–14; John 7:37–39).

entries.title: John
entries.content: John stood at the foot of the cross (John 19:26). He did not just collect stories about Jesus. He witnessed the events and gave an accurate account of the life of Jesus (see John 21:24). This same confidence is also evident in the opening words of John's first letter (1 John 1:1–4).

entries.title: John
entries.content: "Not one of His bones will be broken": God did not allow for the Passover lamb to have broken bones (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Jesus was the final Passover lamb (compare Psalm 34:20; see also 1 Corinthians 5:7).

entries.title: John
entries.content: “They will look on the One they have pierced”: Zechariah 12:10 describes how Israel would look on a prophet or the Messiah and lament their own tragic lack of faith.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• According to Luke's Gospel, Joseph of Arimathea was a brave man "waiting for the kingdom of God" (Luke 23:50–51). He was a wealthy and influential leader in Jerusalem and a member of the Jewish high council (Matthew 27:57; Mark 15:43). He disagreed with the decision to kill Jesus. He asked Pilate for permission to bury Jesus in his own tomb.

• Joseph was a secret disciple (compare John 12:42–43). But his bold action showed his public support for Jesus.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Nicodemus (see John 3:1; John 7:50) was a member of the Jewish high council. He knew these bodies had to be buried before the Sabbath (John 19:31, John 19:42). His public support, like that of Joseph of Arimathea, might show he was becoming a disciple (see study note on 7:49–51). 

• Myrrh was a commonly used powder that smelled good.

• The aloes were fragrant powdered sandalwood often used as perfume. 

• seventy-five pounds: This large amount of spices was fit for royalty. Jesus, the king, received a royal burial.

entries.title: John
entries.content: a new tomb: People have discovered more than 900 first-century burial tombs in Judea, carved into the limestone hills.

entries.title: John
entries.content: because it was the Jewish day of Preparation: See study note on 19:14. It was almost the Sabbath, so Joseph and Nicodemus planned to return later to finish the burial process (John 19:38–39).
