entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Mary Magdalene, a dedicated follower of Jesus, went to the tomb to help finish burying Jesus (see Matthew 27:55–56; Luke 8:1–3; see John 19:42). 

• Many Judean tombs were sealed with a rolling stone.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Mary Magdalene ran to find Simon Peter. She assumed that someone had taken the body of Jesus from the tomb. This kind of tomb disturbance did happen in the ancient world.

entries.title: John
entries.content: The other disciple was likely John, "the one whom Jesus loved" and the author of this Gospel (see John 13:23). He and Peter confirmed Mary's testimony by checking the tomb themselves. John got there first, but Peter went in first.

entries.title: John
entries.content: What Peter and John found in the tomb was remarkable. The linen cloths were on the burial bench (John 19:40). Jews also used a cloth on the face for burials. They rolled it, wrapped it under the chin, and tied it on top of the head (see John 11:44). The apostles found this cloth folded on the bench. John included these details to counter any suggestion that grave robbers had taken the body of Jesus. Thieves would have taken such expensive clothes in a robbery.

entries.title: John
entries.content: he saw and believed: Even though he did not fully understand, John knew God had done this, and he realized Jesus was alive.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Even though two angels appeared inside the tomb, it was still a mystery how Jesus disappeared (see Luke 24:4).

• Why are you weeping?: Sorrow was not the appropriate response in this moment.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Mary thought Jesus was the gardener. Jesus repeated the angel’s question and asked, "Whom are you seeking?" Jesus wanted Mary to think. At this point Mary was looking for the body of Jesus, but she was about to meet the living Christ.

entries.title: John
entries.content: When Jesus called Mary by name, she recognized him immediately (see John 10:3–4).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Mary thought that with the resurrection, Jesus would resume normal relations with his disciples. She was trying to cling to the joy she discovered in her resurrected Lord. But his fellowship with her would come in a new form (John 20:22). Jesus had not yet ascended to complete his return to the Father, but the process was underway. Before his final departure, he would give the Holy Spirit (John 20:22; see John 14:15–21, John 14:26; John 15:26–27; John 16:5–15).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Mary was the first person to see the Lord after his resurrection. She not only saw him, but also heard and touched him (see 1 John 1:1–4). God gave this great honor to a woman whose broken life had experienced healing (Luke 8:2). In Jewish culture, this was surprising. A woman could not even be a witness in court. No Jew at that time would make up such a story.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• the disciples were together with the doors locked: The disciples were afraid that they might be punished for following Jesus.

• Peace be with you!: This was a common Jewish greeting (see also 3 John 1:15). But Jesus was doing more than just greeting his disciples. He was offering the Messiah's peace and delivering the gift of his kingdom (see Isaiah 9:6; Isaiah 52:7; see John 14:27; John 16:33).

entries.title: John
entries.content: The reality that Jesus had been raised from the dead was quite clear. Jesus showed them the wounds from the nails and the spear. He did not fake death but conquered it. He was no ghost but a real man with a real body. He had been dead but was now alive. Jesus was fully human both in life (John 1:14) and in his resurrection.

entries.title: John
entries.content: I am sending you: God sent Jesus into the world to establish his kingdom. Now, Jesus is sending his disciples to continue his mission. Christ's messengers spread the truth of his words to the world (see John 17:18).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
Jesus commissioned his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit. The Spirit had not yet been given earlier, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39). 

After his resurrection, the glorified Jesus gave the Spirit to his followers. This gift fulfilled many promises that the Spirit would be sent (John 14:16, John 14:26; John 15:26; John 16:7, John 16:13). It also points ahead to the Spirit’s powerful coming at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; Acts 2:1–47).

entries.title: John
entries.content: If you forgive anyone his sins: The work of Christ’s followers continues the work of Christ. They do not give or take away God’s forgiveness on their own. Instead, they act according to the guidance of Jesus through the Holy Spirit (John 15:5; John 14:31).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Thomas: See also John 11:16; John 14:5. Thomas was not present when Jesus first appeared. He remained full of doubt even after his friends said they had seen the Lord. Thomas wanted the same direct experience they had.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Eight days later was the first day of the Jewish week (Sunday). This was one week after the resurrection of Jesus. At that time, people included the current day when counting forward. The appearance of Jesus on this Sunday helps explain why the disciples met for worship on "the Lord's Day" (see Revelation 1:10). 

• Peace be with you: This scene was just like the first appearance of Jesus (John 20:19–20). Jesus had already heard the complaint of Thomas, and now Jesus answered directly. 

• believe: Jesus challenged Thomas to believe in the resurrection like the others did.

entries.title: John
entries.content: “My Lord and my God!”: This was not a shout of surprise but a statement of deep faith. It completes John's declaration of Jesus's divinity that has framed the whole book (see John 1:1–18).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus speaks of the generations of Christians who, through the testimony of others, would believe without seeing.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Many scholars think these words are the end of John's Gospel and consider chapter John 21:21 to be an addition. John's account is only a selection of the many miracles and signs Jesus performed.

entries.title: John
entries.content: so that you may believe: Some manuscripts use the present tense, showing that John wrote to encourage those who already believe. Other manuscripts read “that you may [come to] believe,” which suggests that John was helping people begin to have faith (compare John 1:7).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This final chapter includes a story about the resurrected Jesus in Galilee. It describes the conversation between Peter and Jesus about Peter’s love for him (John 21:1–14; John 21:15–23). The chapter concludes by summarizing the authority and importance of John’s eyewitness account (John 21:24–25).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Several of the disciples returned to fishing in the Sea of Galilee. This was not a sign that their faith had weakened. Even rabbis who regularly preached kept practicing their occupations (see Acts 18:3; Acts 20:34; 1 Corinthians 4:12). 

• The sons of Zebedee were James and John (see Matthew 4:21).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Fishing was usually successful in the early hours of the morning. However, this trip was useless and they caught nothing all night.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Jesus was standing on the shore, but the men did not recognize him (compare John 20:11–16; Luke 24:13–53).

entries.title: John
entries.content: Cast the net on the right side: To throw a net into the sea at random would not be helpful. But when they followed the stranger's advice, they caught many fish immediately (John 21:11).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• “It is the Lord!”: John recognized Jesus, likely remembering a similar miracle had happened before (Luke 5:1–11). 

• Peter, who had taken off his clothes while working, put on his tunic (his outer clothing) to meet the Lord.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Cooked fish and bread were the main foods in the diet of those living in Galilee. Jesus offered the men breakfast. The charcoal fire reminds us of when Peter denied Jesus (John 18:18).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This miracle showed generous provision (similar to John 2:1–12; John 6:1–15). The number 153 does not have a symbolic meaning.

entries.title: John
entries.content: None of the disciples dared to ask Him, “Who are You?”: Jesus looked different after God raised him from the dead. After his resurrection, Jesus was truly the same person. Yet his body was transformed and not limited in the same way. When he gave them bread and fish, their doubts disappeared (compare John 6:11; Luke 24:30).

entries.title: John
entries.content: This scene on the beach was the third time Jesus had appeared (see John 20:11–23, John 20:26–29).

entries.title: John
entries.content: more than these? (Or more than these others do?): Jesus reminded Peter of his claim to be more faithful and brave than the others (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). He was urging Peter to examine himself.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• Do you love me?: These three questions and affirmations recall Peter’s three denials (John 18:15–18, John 18:25–27). Jesus invited Peter to reaffirm everything he had denied. 

• The Greek word for love in the first two questions (agapaō) differs from the word in his third question (phileō). In each case, Peter responded with the second word (phileō). Most Greek scholars view the two words as synonyms in this situation.

The conversation Jesus had with Peter focused not on the quality of Peter’s love, but rather on Peter’s task to care for the followers of Jesus. First Peter 5:2–4 might be a meditation on these events.

entries.title: John
entries.content: Feed my sheep: Jesus, who knows everything, understood that despite Peter’s terrible failure, he still had faith and commitment to Jesus (John 1:42; John 2:25; John 16:30). These words called Peter to care for and protect Christ’s followers.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• You will stretch out your hands: Jesus was probably predicting Peter would likewise die on a cross. According to tradition, this is how Peter died. 

• someone else will dress you (literally bind you): Jesus refers to capture, slavery, and crucifixion. They often tied victims to the cross.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• The rest of Peter’s life was a ministry tending the flock of God, and his martyrdom was a kind of death that glorifies God.

• Follow me: This might require suffering and death (see John 13:16; John 15:18–21).

entries.title: John
entries.content:
“Lord, what about him?”: Peter wanted to know if John would also face death for his faith. Jesus said it was not Peter’s concern to know how or when John would die. Peter’s job was to follow Jesus, just as John already was.

This event shows John’s idea of being a disciple: What matters most for the disciple of Jesus is to follow him and do his will, no matter what happens.

entries.title: John
entries.content: What Jesus said to Peter spread, causing some to conclude that John would not die until Jesus returned in his second coming. What Jesus said when he rebuked Peter (John 21:22) is repeated to answer that rumor. Those among the community of believers who believed this rumor were thus instructed to abandon any guessing about what would happen to John. According to tradition, John died peacefully in Ephesus at an old age, surrounded by fellow believers.

entries.title: John
entries.content:
• This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down: John’s Gospel is based on his personal experiences. It is not a story written from rumors or guesses, but from the memories of a man who spent important years with Jesus. He remembered, with the help of the Holy Spirit, what Jesus said and did (John 14:26). 

• we know: This account of the life of Christ was not a guess or from weak memories. Instead, John based it on the confident knowledge of reliable eyewitness accounts.

entries.title: John
entries.content: not even the world itself would have space for the books: John ends his Gospel acknowledging that the story he has described is larger than anything he can imagine or fully communicate. Even though it is wonderful for us to experience, it does not show the full glory of the person he describes. John wants us to know that there is always more to Christ than we can understand.
